entries.name: linearmodels.AbsorbingLS
entries.summary: Linear regression with high-dimensional effects.
keywords: Linear regression with high-dimensional effects. Parameters ---------- dependent : array_like Dependent variable (nobs by 1). exog : array_like, optional Exogenous regressors (nobs by nexog). absorb : DataFrame or Interaction, optional The effects or continuous variables to absorb. When using a DataFrame, effects must be categorical variables. Other variable types are treated as continuous variables that should be absorbed, so they must be numeric, and a ``TypeError`` is raised for columns of strings, which have to be converted to categorical. When using an Interaction, variables in the `cat` argument are treated as effects and variables in the `cont` argument are treated as continuous. interactions : DataFrame, Interaction or list of DataFrame or Interaction, optional Interactions containing both categorical and continuous variables. Each interaction is constructed using the Cartesian product of the categorical variables to produce the dummy, which are then separately interacted with each continuous variable. The columns of a DataFrame follow the rules of ``absorb``. weights : array_like, optional Observation weights used in estimation. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. The default is to weight all observations equally. drop_absorbed : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to drop absorbed variables. The default is False. Raises ------ TypeError If ``absorb`` or ``interactions`` is not a DataFrame or an Interaction (a list of them for ``interactions``), or if a column that is not categorical is not numeric. ValueError If ``dependent``, ``exog``, ``absorb``, ``interactions`` and ``weights`` have different numbers of observations or labels that do not match (see Notes), if all observations have a missing value, or if ``weights`` are not strictly positive and finite. See Also -------- Interaction : Specify interactions between categorical and continuous variables. linearmodels.iv.model.IVLIML : Limited information ML and k-class estimation of IV models. linearmodels.iv.model.IV2SLS : Estimation of IV models using two-stage least squares. scipy.sparse.linalg.lsmr : Iterative solver for sparse least squares problems. Notes ----- Capable of estimating models with millions of effects. The model is not a panel estimator. See :ref:`iv-absorbing-ls` for when to use it and when to use :class:`~linearmodels.panel.model.PanelOLS`. Estimates models of the form .. math:: y_i = x_i \beta + z_i \gamma + \epsilon_i where :math:`\beta` are parameters of interest and :math:`\gamma` are not. z may be high-dimensional, although must have fewer variables than the number of observations in y. The syntax simplifies specifying high-dimensional z when z consists of categorical (factor) variables, also known as effects, or when z contains interactions between continuous variables and categorical variables, also known as fixed slopes. The high-dimensional effects are fit using LSMR which avoids inverting or even constructing the inner product of the regressors. This is combined with Frish-Waugh-Lovell to orthogonalize x and y from z. z can contain factors that are perfectly linearly dependent. LSMR estimates a particular restricted set of parameters that captures the effect of non-redundant components in z. A variable in ``exog`` is absorbed if the effects explain all of it. The algorithms that absorb the effects stop with a relative error of about 1e-8, so a variable is treated as absorbed if less than 1e-5 of its norm is left after the effects are removed, whatever its units. It is treated in the same way if it is collinear with the variables before it once the effects are removed. An ``AbsorbingEffectError`` is raised for such a variable. If ``drop_absorbed`` is True, the variable is dropped and an ``AbsorbingEffectWarning`` is raised, and the constant is never dropped. The norm includes the mean of the variable, so a variable with a large mean and little other variation, less than 1e-5 of its norm, is also treated as absorbed. Subtract its mean to avoid this. Rows are paired by position. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as ``dependent``, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index of ``exog``, ``absorb``, ``interactions`` or ``weights`` differs from the index of ``dependent``. Either reindex the input to the index of ``dependent``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If ``dependent`` does not carry labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of ``exog``, ``absorb``, ``interactions`` and ``weights`` that does. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.BetweenOLS
entries.summary: Between estimator for panel data.
keywords: Between estimator for panel data. Parameters ---------- dependent : PanelData, DataFrame, Series, ndarray or DataArray Dependent (left-hand-side) variable (time by entity). A DataFrame or Series with a 2-level MultiIndex (entity, then time), a DataFrame with time as the index and entities as the columns, a 2-d (time by entity) NumPy array or DataArray, or a PanelData. A list, a tuple or any other container raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``dependent``, since the entities and time periods need labels or a layout. exog : PanelData, DataFrame, Series, ndarray or DataArray Exogenous or right-hand-side variables (variable by time by entity). The containers are those of ``dependent``, where a DataFrame has a column for each variable and an array or DataArray with several variables has 3 dimensions (variable by time by entity). A list, a tuple or any other container raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``exog``. weights : array_like, optional Weights to use in estimation. Assumes the variance of the residual is proportional to the inverse of the weight, so that the residual times the square root of the weight is homoskedastic. Weights can be given for each observation, for each time period, for each entity or for each combination of time period and entity. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. Weights with labels must use the same labels, in the same order, as dependent or, if dependent has no labels, as exog. See :ref:`panel-input-alignment`. Dependent need not be balanced when the weights are given for each time period, entity or combination: the weights of the combinations that dependent does not have are not used. A 1-d array has a value for each row of dependent, in the order of the rows, if it has as many values as dependent has rows. It has a value for each time period if it has as many values as there are time periods, and a value for each entity if it has as many as there are entities. Weights with labels (a pandas object with an index that is not the default index) are read by their labels, so that a Series indexed by the time periods has a value for each time period, and one indexed by the entities has a value for each entity. Weights without labels (an array, a list, a tuple, or a Series or a DataFrame with one column that has the default index) are read by their number of values. If dependent is not balanced and has as many rows as time periods or entities, they have a value for each row. An ``AmbiguityError`` is raised if the numbers of time periods and entities are equal and the weights have that many values, unless they have no labels and a value for each row. Any other number of values raises a ``ValueError``. check_rank : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to perform a rank check on the exogenous variables to ensure that the model is identified. Skipping this check can reduce the time required to validate a model specification. Results may be numerically unstable if this check is skipped and the matrix is not full rank. The default is True. Raises ------ TypeError If `dependent` or `exog` is a container that is not supported, e.g., a list or a tuple, or if they have complex values or values that cannot be converted to float64. ValueError If `dependent`, `exog` or `weights` have different shapes or labels, if a combination of an entity and a time period appears more than once, if the weights are not strictly positive and finite or do not have a supported shape, or if `exog` does not have full column rank and `check_rank` is True. AmbiguityError If the numbers of time periods and entities are equal and 1-d weights have that many values, so that they could be a value for each time period or for each entity. Notes ----- The model is given by .. math:: \bar{y}_{i}= \beta^{\prime}\bar{x}_{i}+\bar{\epsilon}_{i} where :math:`\bar{z}` is the time-average. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weights`` for each time period, each entity or each time period and entity can be used if ``dependent`` is not balanced. Earlier versions raised "weights must have the same number of observations as dependent". .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weights`` that are a 1-d array with a value for each row of ``dependent`` can be used if ``dependent`` is not balanced. Earlier versions raised "Weights do not have a supported shape". An array with a value for each combination of a time period and an entity is not a value for each row if ``dependent`` is not balanced. It raised an error from pandas or NumPy, e.g., "could not broadcast input array from shape (30,1) into shape (27,1)", and raises "Weights do not have a supported shape" now, which names the numbers of values that are accepted. If ``dependent`` is not balanced and has as many rows as time periods or entities, weights without labels (an array, or a Series with the default index) with that many values are a value for each row, and a Series indexed by the time periods or by the entities is a value for each time period or entity. Earlier versions raised "weights must have the same number of observations as dependent", or an ``AmbiguityError`` if the numbers of time periods and entities were equal. A DataFrame with one column and the default index is read as an array with a column is. It raised an error from pandas or NumPy if ``dependent`` was balanced, and "Weights do not have a supported shape" if it was not. A DataFrame with one column and an index that is not the default index is read as a Series with that index is, so that its labels decide. It raised "Weights do not have a supported shape".

entries.name: linearmodels.FamaMacBeth
entries.summary: Fama-MacBeth estimator for panel data.
keywords: Fama-MacBeth estimator for panel data. Parameters ---------- dependent : PanelData, DataFrame, Series, ndarray or DataArray Dependent (left-hand-side) variable (time by entity). A DataFrame or Series with a 2-level MultiIndex (entity, then time), a DataFrame with time as the index and entities as the columns, a 2-d (time by entity) NumPy array or DataArray, or a PanelData. A list, a tuple or any other container raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``dependent``, since the entities and time periods need labels or a layout. exog : PanelData, DataFrame, Series, ndarray or DataArray Exogenous or right-hand-side variables (variable by time by entity). The containers are those of ``dependent``, where a DataFrame has a column for each variable and an array or DataArray with several variables has 3 dimensions (variable by time by entity). A list, a tuple or any other container raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``exog``. weights : array_like, optional Weights to use in estimation. Assumes the variance of the residual is proportional to the inverse of the weight, so that the residual times the square root of the weight is homoskedastic. Weights can be given for each observation, for each time period, for each entity or for each combination of time period and entity. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. Weights with labels must use the same labels, in the same order, as dependent or, if dependent has no labels, as exog. See :ref:`panel-input-alignment`. Dependent need not be balanced when the weights are given for each time period, entity or combination: the weights of the combinations that dependent does not have are not used. A 1-d array has a value for each row of dependent, in the order of the rows, if it has as many values as dependent has rows. It has a value for each time period if it has as many values as there are time periods, and a value for each entity if it has as many as there are entities. Weights with labels (a pandas object with an index that is not the default index) are read by their labels, so that a Series indexed by the time periods has a value for each time period, and one indexed by the entities has a value for each entity. Weights without labels (an array, a list, a tuple, or a Series or a DataFrame with one column that has the default index) are read by their number of values. If dependent is not balanced and has as many rows as time periods or entities, they have a value for each row. An ``AmbiguityError`` is raised if the numbers of time periods and entities are equal and the weights have that many values, unless they have no labels and a value for each row. Any other number of values raises a ``ValueError``. check_rank : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to perform a rank check on the exogenous variables to ensure that the model is identified. Skipping this check can reduce the time required to validate a model specification. Results may be numerically unstable if this check is skipped and the matrix is not full rank. The default is True. Raises ------ TypeError If `dependent` or `exog` is a container that is not supported, e.g., a list or a tuple, or if they have complex values or values that cannot be converted to float64. ValueError If `dependent`, `exog` or `weights` have different shapes or labels, if a combination of an entity and a time period appears more than once, if the weights are not strictly positive and finite or do not have a supported shape, or if `exog` does not have full column rank and `check_rank` is True. It is also raised if none of the cross-sectional regressions can be estimated. AmbiguityError If the numbers of time periods and entities are equal and 1-d weights have that many values, so that they could be a value for each time period or for each entity. Notes ----- The model is given by .. math:: y_{it}=\beta^{\prime}x_{it}+\epsilon_{it} The Fama-MacBeth estimator is computed by performing T regressions, one for each time period using all available entity observations. Denote the estimate of the model parameters as :math:`\hat{\beta}_t`. The reported estimator is then .. math:: \hat{\beta} = T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T \hat{\beta}_t While the model does not explicitly include time-effects, the implementation based on regressing all observation in a single time period is "as-if" time effects are included. Each period needs at least as many entities as regressors, and the regressors must vary across the entities of the period, so that they are not collinear: a regressor that depends only on time is collinear with the constant. Periods whose cross-section is rank deficient are dropped with a warning, and T counts only the periods that are used. It is an error if no period can be used. Parameter inference is made using the set of T parameter estimates with either the standard covariance estimator or a kernel-based covariance, depending on ``cov_type``. Since the parameters are the averages of the T cross-sectional estimates, the t-statistics are compared with a t distribution with T - 1 degrees of freedom, which is the convention of Fama and MacBeth [1]_. T is the number of periods whose cross-sectional regression is estimated. The p-values and confidence intervals use this distribution if ``debiased`` is True, which is the default, and the normal distribution otherwise. The joint test that the k parameters other than the constant are zero, ``f_statistic_robust`` of the results, is the Hotelling T-squared test [2]_. The Wald statistic W of the k parameters is multiplied by (T - k) / (k (T - 1)) and compared with an F distribution with k and T - k degrees of freedom if ``debiased`` is True, and W is compared with a chi-squared distribution with k degrees of freedom otherwise. The F test is exact if the T estimates are independent draws from the same normal distribution and ``cov_type`` is not "kernel". With the kernel covariance it is only an approximation, which can reject a true null hypothesis far too often when T is small. With one tested parameter it is the squared t-statistic, with the p-value of the t distribution with T - 1 degrees of freedom. An F distribution with k and T - 1 degrees of freedom, or with the degrees of freedom of the pooled regression, rejects a true null hypothesis too often when k is larger than 1, see :attr:`~linearmodels.panel.results.FamaMacBethResults.f_statistic_robust`. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weights`` for each time period, each entity or each time period and entity can be used if ``dependent`` is not balanced. Earlier versions raised "weights must have the same number of observations as dependent". .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weights`` that are a 1-d array with a value for each row of ``dependent`` can be used if ``dependent`` is not balanced. Earlier versions raised "Weights do not have a supported shape". An array with a value for each combination of a time period and an entity is not a value for each row if ``dependent`` is not balanced. It raised an error from pandas or NumPy, e.g., "could not broadcast input array from shape (30,1) into shape (27,1)", and raises "Weights do not have a supported shape" now, which names the numbers of values that are accepted. If ``dependent`` is not balanced and has as many rows as time periods or entities, weights without labels (an array, or a Series with the default index) with that many values are a value for each row, and a Series indexed by the time periods or by the entities is a value for each time period or entity. Earlier versions raised "weights must have the same number of observations as dependent", or an ``AmbiguityError`` if the numbers of time periods and entities were equal. A DataFrame with one column and the default index is read as an array with a column is. It raised an error from pandas or NumPy if ``dependent`` was balanced, and "Weights do not have a supported shape" if it was not. A DataFrame with one column and an index that is not the default index is read as a Series with that index is, so that its labels decide. It raised "Weights do not have a supported shape". References ---------- .. [1] Fama, E. F. and MacBeth, J. D. (1973). Risk, return, and equilibrium: Empirical tests. Journal of Political Economy, 81(3), 607-636. .. [2] Hotelling, H. (1931). The generalization of Student's ratio. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 2(3), 360-378.

entries.name: linearmodels.IV2SLS
entries.summary: Estimation of IV models using two-stage least squares.
keywords: Estimation of IV models using two-stage least squares. Parameters ---------- dependent : array_like Dependent variable (nobs by 1). exog : array_like or None Exogenous regressors (nobs by nexog). None if the model has no exogenous regressors. endog : array_like or None Endogenous regressors (nobs by nendog). None if the model has no endogenous regressors. instruments : array_like or None Instrumental variables (nobs by ninstr). None if the model has no instruments. weights : array_like, optional Observation weights used in estimation. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. The default is to weight all observations equally. Raises ------ ValueError If the model has no regressors, if there are fewer instruments than endogenous regressors, if ``[exog, endog]`` or ``[exog, instruments]`` does not have full column rank, if all observations have a missing value, if the inputs have different numbers of observations or labels that do not match (see Notes), or if ``weights`` are not strictly positive and finite. TypeError If an input is complex or cannot be converted to float64. See Also -------- IVLIML : Limited information ML and k-class estimation of IV models. IVGMM : Estimation of IV models using the generalized method of moments. IVGMMCUE : Estimation of IV models using continuously updating GMM. Notes ----- The 2SLS estimator is defined .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{2SLS} & =(X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X)^{-1}X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y\\ & =(\hat{X}'\hat{X})^{-1}\hat{X}'Y\\ \hat{X} & =Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X The 2SLS estimator is a special case of a k-class estimator with :math:`\kappa=1`, The estimates do not use the estimate of :math:`\kappa` of LIML, but the Anderson-Rubin and Basmann F tests of overidentification of the results do. The estimate of :math:`\kappa` is not defined if there are fewer than :math:`1 + n_{endog}` observations more than the number of exogenous regressors and instruments, or if the residuals of the dependent variable and the endogenous regressors on the exogenous regressors and instruments are collinear (see :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVLIML`). The model is estimated then, and the tests are an ``InvalidTestStatistic``. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The Anderson-Rubin and Basmann F tests are an ``InvalidTestStatistic`` if :math:`\kappa` is not defined. Earlier versions computed them from the rounding error of a singular matrix, or the statistics were NaN. Rows are paired by position. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as ``dependent``, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` or ``weights`` differs from the index of ``dependent``. Either reindex the input to the index of ``dependent``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If ``dependent`` does not carry labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` that does. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels. .. todo:: * VCV: bootstrap

entries.name: linearmodels.IV3SLS
entries.summary: Three-stage Least Squares (3SLS) Estimator.
keywords: Three-stage Least Squares (3SLS) Estimator. Parameters ---------- equations : dict of str to tuple or dict Dictionary-like structure containing dependent, exogenous, endogenous and instrumental variables. Each key is an equations label and must be a string. Each value must be either a tuple of the form (dependent, exog, endog, instrument[, weights]) or a dictionary with keys "dependent", and at least one of "exog" or "endog" and "instruments". When using a tuple, values must be provided for all 4 variables, although either empty arrays or `None` can be passed if a category of variable is not included in a model. The dictionary may contain optional keys for "exog", "endog", "instruments", and "weights". "exog" can be omitted if all variables in an equation are endogenous. Alternatively, "exog" can contain either an empty array or `None` to indicate that an equation contains no exogenous regressors. Similarly "endog" and "instruments" can either be omitted or may contain an empty array (or `None`) if all variables in an equation are exogenous. The variables are array_like, such as lists, NumPy arrays, pandas objects and xarray DataArrays, and a ``TypeError`` that names the variable is raised for complex values or text. sigma : array_like, optional Prespecified residual covariance to use in GLS estimation, with shape (nequations, nequations). If not provided, FGLS is implemented based on an estimate of sigma. Notes ----- Estimates a set of regressions which are seemingly unrelated in the sense that separate estimation would lead to consistent parameter estimates. Each equation is of the form .. math:: y_{i,k} = x_{i,k}\beta_i + \epsilon_{i,k} where k denotes the equation and i denoted the observation index. By stacking vertically arrays of dependent and placing the exogenous variables into a block diagonal array, the entire system can be compactly expressed as .. math:: Y = X\beta + \epsilon where .. math:: Y = \left[\begin{array}{c}Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_K\end{array}\right] and .. math:: X = \left[\begin{array}{cccc} X_1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\ 0 & X_2 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & X_K \end{array}\right] The system instrumental variable (IV) estimator is .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{IV} & = (X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X)^{-1}X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y \\ & = (\hat{X}'\hat{X})^{-1}\hat{X}'Y where :math:`\hat{X} = Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X`. When certain conditions are satisfied, a GLS estimator of the form .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{3SLS} = (\hat{X}'\Omega^{-1}\hat{X})^{-1}\hat{X}'\Omega^{-1}Y can improve accuracy of coefficient estimates where .. math:: \Omega = \Sigma \otimes I_N where :math:`\Sigma` is the covariance matrix of the residuals. The weights of an equation, if they are given, must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1 in the equation. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped from all of the equations. Rows are paired by position, both within an equation and across the equations. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as the dependent variable of its equation, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. The dependent variables that carry labels must also use the same index in every equation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if an index differs. Either reindex the input to the index of the dependent variable, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If none of the dependent variables carries labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of them that does, in the order ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` of each equation. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.IVGMM
entries.summary: Estimation of IV models using the generalized method of moments (GMM).
keywords: Estimation of IV models using the generalized method of moments (GMM). Parameters ---------- dependent : array_like Dependent variable (nobs by 1). exog : array_like or None Exogenous regressors (nobs by nexog). None if the model has no exogenous regressors. endog : array_like or None Endogenous regressors (nobs by nendog). None if the model has no endogenous regressors. instruments : array_like or None Instrumental variables (nobs by ninstr). None if the model has no instruments. weights : array_like, optional Observation weights used in estimation. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. The default is to weight all observations equally. weight_type : str, optional Name of moment condition weight function to use in the GMM estimation. The default is "robust". The names are not case sensitive. The supported weight functions are: * "unadjusted", "homoskedastic" * "robust", "heteroskedastic" * "kernel" * "clustered", "one-way" See Notes for their assumptions. **weight_config : dict Additional keyword arguments to pass to the moment condition weight function. The keys are ``center`` (bool) and ``debiased`` (bool) for every weight function, ``kernel`` (str), ``bandwidth`` (int) and ``optimal_bw`` (bool) for "kernel", and ``clusters`` (array_like) for "clustered". The names of the kernels are not case sensitive. ``clusters`` is required and has one element for each observation. See :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.HomoskedasticWeightMatrix`, :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.HeteroskedasticWeightMatrix`, :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix` and :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.OneWayClusteredWeightMatrix` for the details. Raises ------ ValueError If the model has no regressors, if there are fewer instruments than endogenous regressors, if ``[exog, endog]`` or ``[exog, instruments]`` does not have full column rank, if all observations have a missing value, if the inputs have different numbers of observations or labels that do not match (see Notes), or if ``weights`` are not strictly positive and finite. UnknownOptionError If ``weight_type`` is not supported, or if it is "kernel" and ``kernel`` is not a supported kernel. It is both a ``KeyError`` and a ``ValueError``. Before 7.1, an unsupported ``kernel`` was reported by ``fit``. TypeError If an input is complex or cannot be converted to float64. See Also -------- IV2SLS : Estimation of IV models using two-stage least squares. IVLIML : Limited information ML and k-class estimation of IV models. IVGMMCUE : Estimation of IV models using continuously updating GMM. Notes ----- Available GMM weight functions are: * "unadjusted", "homoskedastic" - Assumes moment conditions are homoskedastic * "robust", "heteroskedastic" - Allows for heteroskedasticity but not autocorrelation * "kernel" - Allows for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation * "clustered", "one-way" - Allows for one-way cluster dependence The estimator is defined as .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{gmm}=(X'ZW^{-1}Z'X)^{-1}X'ZW^{-1}Z'Y where :math:`W` is a positive definite weight matrix and :math:`Z` contains both the exogenous regressors and the instruments. The bandwidth of a kernel weight matrix (``weight_type="kernel"``) is ``bandwidth`` if it is given in ``weight_config``. If neither ``bandwidth`` nor ``optimal_bw`` is given, it is estimated from the data, as the bandwidth of the kernel covariance of :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IV2SLS` and :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVLIML` is. In 7.0 and earlier it was ``nobs - 2``, which is not a consistent estimator, so the estimates, standard errors and J statistic can be different. ``fit`` issues a ``DefaultBandwidthWarning`` (a ``UserWarning``) when it uses the default. To restore the previous behavior, pass ``optimal_bw=False`` or ``bandwidth=nobs - 2`` in ``weight_config``, for example ``IVGMM(dependent, exog, endog, instruments, weight_type="kernel", optimal_bw=False)``. Passing ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw`` silences the warning, and ``optimal_bw=True`` selects the bandwidth from the data without it. The same holds for ``cov_type="kernel"`` in ``fit``. See :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix` and :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.IVGMMCovariance`. The bandwidth that is estimated from the data needs at least 4 observations with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel. ``fit`` raises a ``ValueError`` for fewer observations, and if the estimated bandwidth is not finite. Pass ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw=False`` to use the kernel with fewer observations. See :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`. Rows are paired by position. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as ``dependent``, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` or ``weights`` differs from the index of ``dependent``. Either reindex the input to the index of ``dependent``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If ``dependent`` does not carry labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` that does. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit`` or in ``weight_config``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels. The weight matrix is the inverse of an estimate of the covariance of the moment conditions, so that the estimate has to be nonsingular. A clustered estimate from G clusters has rank at most G, and at most G - 1 if the moment conditions are centered (``center`` is ``True``), since the centered cluster sums add to zero. There have to be at least as many clusters as moment conditions, and more if they are centered. The first step moment conditions of an exactly identified model add to zero as well, so that it needs more clusters than moment conditions with every value of ``center``. The rank of a kernel or robust estimate is bounded in the same way by the number of observations. ``fit`` raises a ``ValueError`` that says so if the estimate is singular, since the estimates would be numerical noise. The estimate is not used, and so it is not tested, if ``iter_limit`` is 1. .. todo:: * VCV: bootstrap

IVGMM : Estimation of IV models using the generalized method of moments. entries.name: linearmodels.IVJIVE
entries.summary: Jackknife instrumental variables estimator (JIVE).
keywords: Jackknife instrumental variables estimator (JIVE). Parameters ---------- dependent : array_like Dependent variable (nobs by 1). exog : array_like or None Exogenous regressors (nobs by nexog). None if the model has no exogenous regressors. endog : array_like or None Endogenous regressors (nobs by nendog). None if the model has no endogenous regressors. instruments : array_like or None Instrumental variables (nobs by ninstr). None if the model has no instruments. weights : array_like, optional Observation weights used in estimation. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. The default is to weight all observations equally. Raises ------ ValueError If the model has no regressors, if there are fewer instruments than endogenous regressors, if ``[exog, endog]`` or ``[exog, instruments]`` does not have full column rank, if all observations have a missing value, if the inputs have different numbers of observations or labels that do not match (see Notes), or if ``weights`` are not strictly positive and finite. TypeError If an input is complex or cannot be converted to float64. See Also -------- IV2SLS : Estimation of IV models using two-stage least squares. IVLIML : Limited information ML and k-class estimation of IV models. IVGMM : Estimation of IV models using the generalized method of moments. IVGMMCUE : Estimation of IV models using continuously updating GMM. Notes ----- JIVE replaces the 2SLS first-stage fitted values :math:`\hat{X}=P_ZX` with leave-one-out predictions. The prediction for observation :math:`i` is the fitted value from a first stage regression that does not use observation :math:`i` .. math:: \tilde{x}_i = \frac{\hat{x}_i - h_i x_i}{1 - h_i}, \qquad h_i = z_i'(Z'Z)^{-1}z_i, where :math:`Z` contains the exogenous regressors and the instruments and :math:`h_i` is the leverage of observation :math:`i`. The estimator is .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{JIVE} = (\tilde{X}'X)^{-1} \tilde{X}'y. This is the estimator that is called JIVE1 by Angrist, Imbens and Krueger (1999). Exogenous regressors are in :math:`Z`, so they are their own leave-one-out predictions. In a weighted model the estimator is applied to the data that has been multiplied by the square root of the weights. The leverages are used to compute :math:`\tilde{X}` without estimating :math:`n` regressions, using a QR decomposition of :math:`Z`. The estimator cannot be computed if an observation has a leverage of 1, which happens if it is the only observation that has a non-zero value of one of the instruments, e.g., a dummy variable that is 1 for a single observation. The covariance estimators are the same as in the other IV models, and are computed using :math:`\tilde{X}` as the instruments. See :meth:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVJIVE.fit`. These are valid when the number of instruments is small relative to the strength of the first stage. They can understate the uncertainty when there are many instruments (see Chao, Swanson, Hausman, Newey and Woutersen, 2012). JIVE reduces the many instruments bias of 2SLS, but it can have a larger variance, particularly when the instruments are weak (see Davidson and MacKinnon, 2006). The estimates do not use the estimate of :math:`\kappa` of LIML, but the Anderson-Rubin and Basmann F tests of overidentification of the results do. The estimate of :math:`\kappa` is not defined if there are fewer than :math:`1 + n_{endog}` observations more than the number of exogenous regressors and instruments, or if the residuals of the dependent variable and the endogenous regressors on the exogenous regressors and instruments are collinear (see :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVLIML`). The model is estimated then, and the tests are an ``InvalidTestStatistic``. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The Anderson-Rubin and Basmann F tests are an ``InvalidTestStatistic`` if :math:`\kappa` is not defined. Earlier versions computed them from the rounding error of a singular matrix, or the statistics were NaN. Rows are paired by position. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as ``dependent``, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` or ``weights`` differs from the index of ``dependent``. Either reindex the input to the index of ``dependent``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If ``dependent`` does not carry labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` that does. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels. References ---------- Angrist, J. D., Imbens, G. W., & Krueger, A. B. (1999). Jackknife instrumental variables estimation. *Journal of Applied Econometrics*, 14(1), 57-67. Chao, J. C., Swanson, N. R., Hausman, J. A., Newey, W. K., & Woutersen, T. (2012). Asymptotic distribution of JIVE in a heteroskedastic IV regression with many instruments. *Econometric Theory*, 28(1), 42-86. Davidson, R., & MacKinnon, J. G. (2006). The case against JIVE. *Journal of Applied Econometrics*, 21(6), 827-833.

entries.summary: Limited information ML and k-class estimation of IV models.
keywords: Limited information ML and k-class estimation of IV models. Parameters ---------- dependent : array_like Dependent variable (nobs by 1). exog : array_like or None Exogenous regressors (nobs by nexog). Notes ----- ``kappa`` and ``fuller`` should not be used simultaneously since Fuller's alpha applies an adjustment to ``kappa``, and so the same result can be computed using only ``kappa``. Fuller's alpha is used to adjust the LIML estimate of :math:`\kappa`, which is computed whenever ``kappa`` is not provided. The LIML estimator is defined as .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{\kappa} & =(X(I-\kappa M_{z})X)^{-1}X(I-\kappa M_{z})Y\\ M_{z} & =I-P_{z}\\ P_{z} & =Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z' where :math:`Z` contains both the exogenous regressors and the instruments. :math:`\kappa` is estimated as part of the LIML estimator. When using Fuller's :math:`\alpha`, the value used is modified to .. math:: \kappa-\alpha/(n-n_{instr}) :math:`\kappa` is the smallest eigenvalue of the cross product of the residuals of the dependent variable and the endogenous regressors on the exogenous regressors, relative to the cross product of their residuals on the exogenous regressors and the instruments, which is inverted. It is not defined if the residuals on the exogenous regressors and the instruments are linearly dependent. That occurs if there are fewer than :math:`1 + n_{endog}` observations more than the number of exogenous regressors and instruments (for example, fewer than 4 observations for a constant, one endogenous regressor and one instrument), and if the residuals are collinear for another reason. Whether the residuals are collinear does not depend on the units of the variables. ``fit`` raises a ``ValueError`` if ``kappa`` is not provided and :math:`\kappa` is not defined. The model is estimated if ``kappa`` is provided, and then the Anderson-Rubin and Basmann F tests of overidentification of the results are an ``InvalidTestStatistic``, since they use the estimate of :math:`\kappa`. Two cases are not covered, see :issue:`823`. An endogenous regressor that is exactly a linear combination of the exogenous regressors and instruments has residuals that are only rounding error, and so does :math:`\kappa`. With 2 or more endogenous regressors, :math:`\kappa` loses accuracy, and the estimate can fail, if the variables are on very different scales. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A ``ValueError`` is raised if :math:`\kappa` is not defined. Earlier versions used the rounding error of the singular cross product, for example 0.8125 instead of 1 in a just-identified model with 3 observations, a constant, one endogenous regressor and one instrument. If ``dependent`` does not carry labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` that does. entries.name: linearmodels.IVSystemGMM
entries.summary: System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimation of linear IV models.
keywords: System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimation of linear IV models. Parameters ---------- equations : dict of str to tuple or dict Dictionary-like structure containing dependent, exogenous, endogenous and instrumental variables. Each key is an equations label and must be a string. Each value must be either a tuple of the form (dependent, exog, endog, instrument[, weights]) or a dictionary with keys "dependent", "exog". The dictionary may contain optional keys for "endog", "instruments", and "weights". Endogenous and/or Instrument can be empty if all variables in an equation are exogenous. The variables are array_like, such as lists, NumPy arrays, pandas objects and xarray DataArrays, and a ``TypeError`` that names the variable is raised for complex values or text. sigma : array_like, optional Prespecified residual covariance to use in GLS estimation, with shape (nequations, nequations). If not provided, FGLS is implemented based on an estimate of sigma. Only used if weight_type is "unadjusted" or "homoskedastic". A ``UserWarning`` is issued, and sigma is ignored, if it is provided with another weight type. weight_type : str, optional Name of moment condition weight function to use in the GMM estimation. The default is "robust". The names are not case sensitive. The supported weight functions are: * "unadjusted", "homoskedastic" - Assume moments are homoskedastic * "robust", "heteroskedastic" - Allow for heteroskedasticity * "kernel", "hac" - Allow for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation **weight_config : dict Additional keyword arguments to pass to the moment condition weight function. All weight types accept ``center`` (bool), whether to center the moment conditions, and ``debiased`` (bool), whether to use small-sample adjustments. Both are False by default. "kernel" also accepts ``kernel`` (str), the name of the kernel, which is "bartlett" if it is not provided, ``bandwidth`` (float), and ``optimal_bw`` (bool). The names of the kernels are not case sensitive. See :class:`~linearmodels.system.gmm.HomoskedasticWeightMatrix`, :class:`~linearmodels.system.gmm.HeteroskedasticWeightMatrix` and :class:`~linearmodels.system.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix` for the details. Raises ------ UnknownOptionError If ``weight_type`` is not supported or ``kernel`` is not a supported kernel. It is both a ``KeyError`` and a ``ValueError``. Notes ----- Estimates a linear model using GMM. Each equation is of the form .. math:: y_{i,k} = x_{i,k}\beta_i + \epsilon_{i,k} where k denotes the equation and i denoted the observation index. By stacking vertically arrays of dependent and placing the exogenous variables into a block diagonal array, the entire system can be compactly expressed as .. math:: Y = X\beta + \epsilon where .. math:: Y = \left[\begin{array}{c}Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_K\end{array}\right] and .. math:: X = \left[\begin{array}{cccc} X_1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\ 0 & X_2 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & X_K \end{array}\right] The system GMM estimator uses the moment condition .. math:: z_{ij}(y_{ij} - x_{ij}\beta_j) = 0 where j indexes the equation. The estimator for the coefficients is given by .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{GMM} & = (X'ZW^{-1}Z'X)^{-1}X'ZW^{-1}Z'Y \\ where :math:`W` is a positive definite weighting matrix. The weight matrix is the inverse of an estimate of the covariance of the moment conditions. ``weight_type`` selects the estimator: "unadjusted" ("homoskedastic"), "robust" ("heteroskedastic") or "kernel" (``"hac"``), and ``weight_config`` contains its options. These are ``center`` and ``debiased`` for all of them, and ``kernel``, ``bandwidth`` and ``optimal_bw`` for "kernel". The bandwidth of a kernel weight matrix (``weight_type="kernel"``) is ``bandwidth`` if it is given in ``weight_config``, and ``nobs - 2`` if ``optimal_bw`` is ``False``. Otherwise, which is the default and what ``optimal_bw=True`` does, it is estimated from the data, from the residuals that the weight matrix is computed from. These are the residuals of the first step estimates in two-step GMM, which is the default. A bandwidth that is estimated from the data, for the weight matrix or the covariance, needs at least 4 observations with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel. ``fit`` raises a ``ValueError`` for fewer observations, and if the estimated bandwidth is not finite. Pass ``bandwidth`` to use the kernel with fewer observations. See :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`. In 7.0 and earlier the default was ``nobs - 2``, which is not a consistent estimator of the covariance of the moment conditions, so the estimates, standard errors and J statistic can be different. ``fit`` issues a ``DefaultBandwidthWarning`` (a ``UserWarning``) when it uses the default. To restore the previous behavior, pass ``optimal_bw=False`` or ``bandwidth=nobs - 2``, where ``nobs`` is the number of observations of each equation, in ``weight_config``, for example ``IVSystemGMM(equations, weight_type="kernel", optimal_bw=False)``. Passing ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw`` silences the warning, and ``optimal_bw=True`` selects the bandwidth from the data without it. The kernel covariance of the parameters (``cov_type="kernel"`` in ``fit``) is not affected, since it has always estimated its bandwidth from the data unless ``bandwidth`` is given. See :class:`~linearmodels.system.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix`. The weights of an equation, if they are given, must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1 in the equation. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped from all of the equations. Rows are paired by position, both within an equation and across the equations. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as the dependent variable of its equation, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. The dependent variables that carry labels must also use the same index in every equation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if an index differs. Either reindex the input to the index of the dependent variable, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If none of the dependent variables carries labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of them that does, in the order ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` of each equation. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.LinearFactorModel
entries.summary: Linear factor model estimator.
keywords: Linear factor model estimator. Parameters ---------- portfolios : array_like Test portfolio returns (nobs by nportfolio). factors : array_like Priced factor returns (nobs by nfactor). risk_free : bool, optional Flag indicating whether the risk-free rate should be estimated from returns along other risk premia. If False, the returns are assumed to be excess returns using the correct risk-free rate. The default is False. sigma : array_like, optional Positive definite residual covariance (nportfolio by nportfolio) that weights the test portfolios in the second stage. A ``ValueError`` is raised if it does not have this shape, contains missing or infinite values, or is not symmetric and positive definite. If not provided, the identity matrix is used. Notes ----- Suitable for traded or non-traded factors. Implements a 2-step estimator of risk premia, factor loadings and model tests. The first stage model estimated is .. math:: r_{it} = c_i + f_t \beta_i + \epsilon_{it} where :math:`r_{it}` is the return on test portfolio i and :math:`f_t` are the traded factor returns. The parameters :math:`c_i` are required to allow non-traded to be tested, but are not economically interesting. These are not reported. The second stage model uses the estimated factor loadings from the first and is .. math:: \bar{r}_i = \lambda_0 + \hat{\beta}_i^\prime \lambda + \eta_i where :math:`\bar{r}_i` is the average excess return to portfolio i and :math:`\lambda_0` is only included if estimating the risk-free rate. GLS is used in the second stage if ``sigma`` is provided. The model is tested using the estimated values :math:`\hat{\alpha}_i=\hat{\eta}_i`, the pricing errors. With :math:`N` test portfolios, :math:`K` factors and :math:`n_{rf}` equal to 1 if the risk-free rate is estimated and 0 if it is not, the second stage estimates make the pricing errors orthogonal to the :math:`K + n_{rf}` columns of :math:`\Sigma^{-1}\hat{\beta}_c`. Here :math:`\hat{\beta}_c` contains the estimated factor loadings, preceded by a column of ones if the risk-free rate is estimated, and :math:`\Sigma` is ``sigma``, or the identity if it is not provided. The pricing errors therefore lie in a space with :math:`N - K - n_{rf}` dimensions, and the covariance of the pricing errors has rank :math:`N - K - n_{rf}`. The J-statistic is the Wald statistic of the pricing errors in the space where they lie, .. math:: J = (Q^\prime\hat{\alpha})^\prime (Q^\prime \hat{V} Q)^{-1} (Q^\prime\hat{\alpha}) where :math:`\hat{V}` is the estimated covariance of the pricing errors and :math:`Q` is an :math:`N` by :math:`N - K - n_{rf}` matrix whose orthonormal columns span the space that is orthogonal to the columns of :math:`\Sigma^{-1}\hat{\beta}_c`. The :math:`N - K - n_{rf}` elements of :math:`Q^\prime\hat{\alpha}` are the coordinates of the pricing errors in that space, and :math:`Q^\prime \hat{V} Q` is their estimated covariance. The statistic tests the null that all of the pricing errors are zero, and has an asymptotic :math:`\chi^2_{N-K-n_{rf}}` distribution. It can also be written :math:`\hat{\alpha}^\prime \hat{V}^{+} \hat{\alpha}` for :math:`\hat{V}^{+}=Q(Q^\prime \hat{V} Q)^{-1}Q^\prime`, which has rank :math:`N - K - n_{rf}`. If :math:`\hat{V}` were exactly singular in the directions of the columns of :math:`\Sigma^{-1}\hat{\beta}_c`, as the covariance of the pricing errors is in theory, :math:`\hat{V}^{+}` would be its Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse. In a sample, :math:`\hat{V}` is not exactly singular. The Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of :math:`\hat{V}` would either invert the directions that are null in theory, which makes the statistic too large, or need a tolerance that decides which eigenvalues are treated as zero. The J-statistic instead projects the pricing errors on the space where they lie and uses the rank that the model implies, :math:`N - K - n_{rf}`, so that no tolerance decides which eigenvalues are treated as zero. The statistic depends on the space and not on the basis of the space: any other orthonormal basis, :math:`QR` for an orthogonal matrix :math:`R`, gives the same value. It therefore does not depend on the order of the test portfolios. Reordering the columns of ``portfolios``, and the rows and columns of ``sigma`` in the same way, reorders :math:`\hat{\alpha}`, :math:`\hat{V}` and the rows of :math:`\Sigma^{-1}\hat{\beta}_c` in the same way and does not change the statistic. It also does not depend on the order of the observations if ``cov_type`` is ``"robust"``, but the kernel covariance estimators use the order of the observations. If :math:`Q^\prime \hat{V} Q` is numerically singular, which can occur when there are few observations, the J-statistic is an ``InvalidTestStatistic``. If the number of test portfolios is the number of risk premia, :math:`N = K + n_{rf}`, the pricing errors are zero and the statistic is 0 with 0 degrees of freedom. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The J-statistic used the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of :math:`\hat{V}` with its default tolerance, which also inverts the directions in which the covariance is null in theory. Its eigenvalues are small but not zero in a sample. The statistic was therefore too large: by 4% in the median and by up to 30% in 200 simulated samples of a correct model with 250 observations, 25 portfolios and 3 factors, where the 5% test rejected 12.5% of the samples (10.0% now; with 1,000 observations 7.5% and 5.5%). The covariance can be far from singular in those directions when there are few portfolios: the J-statistic of the five portfolios and three factors of the Fama-French example in the documentation is 41.6 and was 100.6. If the risk-free rate was estimated, an eigenvalue that is numerically zero was inverted as well, and the statistic changed in the third digit when the observations were only reordered. Rows are paired by position, so that the first row of ``factors`` is the factor return in the period of the first row of ``portfolios``. If both ``portfolios`` and ``factors`` carry labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates), ``factors`` must use the same index, in the same order, as ``portfolios``, so that a return cannot be attached to the wrong period. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index differs. Either reindex ``factors`` to the index of ``portfolios``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.LinearFactorModelGMM
entries.summary: GMM estimator of Linear factor models.
keywords: GMM estimator of Linear factor models. Parameters ---------- portfolios : array_like Test portfolio returns (nobs by nportfolio). factors : array_like Priced factors values (nobs by nfactor). risk_free : bool, optional Flag indicating whether the risk-free rate should be estimated from returns along other risk premia. If False, the returns are assumed to be excess returns using the correct risk-free rate. The default is False. Notes ----- Suitable for traded or non-traded factors. Implements a GMM estimator of risk premia, factor loadings and model tests. The moments are .. math:: \left[\begin{array}{c} \epsilon_{t}\otimes f_{c,t}\\ f_{t}-\mu \end{array}\right] and .. math:: \epsilon_{t}=r_{t}-\left[1_{N}\;\beta\right]\lambda-\beta\left(f_{t}-\mu\right) where :math:`r_{it}` is the return on test portfolio i and :math:`f_t` are the factor returns. There are :math:`N (K + 1) + K` moment conditions, where :math:`N` is the number of test portfolios and :math:`K` is the number of factors. The number of observations must exceed the number of moment conditions, since the covariance of the moment conditions, which weights them, is singular otherwise. A ``ValueError`` is raised if it does not. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A ``ValueError`` is raised if the number of observations does not exceed the number of moment conditions. The estimator raised a ``LinAlgError`` or returned a J-statistic that was NaN or arbitrary, such as -4.6e35. The model is tested using the optimized objective function using the usual GMM J statistic. The alphas are the averages of the moment conditions :math:`\epsilon_t` that correspond to the intercept, and their standard errors account for the estimation of the parameters. If :math:`S` is the covariance of the moment conditions and :math:`G` is the Jacobian of their average, the covariance of the average moment conditions at the efficient GMM estimates is .. math:: \left(S - G (G^\prime S^{-1} G)^{-1} G^\prime\right) / (T - df) where :math:`df` is the number of factors if the covariance is debiased and 0 if it is not. This is the same :math:`S`, :math:`G` and scale as the covariance of the parameters :math:`(G^\prime S^{-1} G)^{-1} / (T - df)`, which depends on ``cov_type`` (and ``kernel`` and ``bandwidth`` for the kernel estimator), ``center`` and ``debiased`` of ``fit``. The covariance of the alphas has rank equal to the number of degrees of freedom of the J-statistic. If the model is just identified, the alphas are zero and so is their variance. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The standard errors of the alphas were the square roots of the diagonal of the covariance of the average moment conditions, :math:`S / T`, which ignores that the parameters were estimated, and which did not depend on ``cov_type``, ``center`` or ``debiased``. This overstated the standard errors: in a simulation of 60 samples with 400 observations, 6 portfolios and 2 factors the mean standard error was 0.00143 to 0.00145 for all six alphas, where their sampling standard deviations were 0.00047 to 0.00136. The mean standard errors are now 0.00049 to 0.00133 and track them. The t-statistics and p-values of the alphas, which are in ``tstats`` and ``pvalues``, change with them. The covariance of the parameters, the risk premia and the J-statistic do not change. Rows are paired by position, so that the first row of ``factors`` is the factor return in the period of the first row of ``portfolios``. If both ``portfolios`` and ``factors`` carry labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates), ``factors`` must use the same index, in the same order, as ``portfolios``, so that a return cannot be attached to the wrong period. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index differs. Either reindex ``factors`` to the index of ``portfolios``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.OLS
entries.summary: Compute OLS estimates when required.
keywords: Compute OLS estimates when required. Private class used when model reduces to OLS. Should use the statsmodels version when needing a supported public API. Parameters ---------- dependent : array_like Dependent variable (nobs by 1). exog : array_like Exogenous regressors (nobs by nexog). weights : array_like, optional Observation weights used in estimation. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. The default is to weight all observations equally. See Also -------- statsmodels.regression.linear_model.OLS : Ordinary least squares. statsmodels.regression.linear_model.GLS : Generalized least squares. Notes ----- Uses IV2SLS internally by setting endog and instruments to None. Uses IVLIML with kappa=0 to estimate OLS models. Rows are paired by position. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as ``dependent``, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index of ``exog`` or ``weights`` differs from the index of ``dependent``. Either reindex the input to the index of ``dependent``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If ``dependent`` does not carry labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of ``exog`` and ``weights`` that does. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.PanelOLS
entries.summary: One- and two-way fixed effects estimator for panel data.
keywords: One- and two-way fixed effects estimator for panel data. Parameters ---------- dependent : PanelData, DataFrame, Series, ndarray or DataArray Dependent (left-hand-side) variable (time by entity). A DataFrame or Series with a 2-level MultiIndex (entity, then time), a DataFrame with time as the index and entities as the columns, a 2-d (time by entity) NumPy array or DataArray, or a PanelData. A list, a tuple or any other container raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``dependent``, since the entities and time periods need labels or a layout. exog : PanelData, DataFrame, Series, ndarray or DataArray Exogenous or right-hand-side variables (variable by time by entity). The containers are those of ``dependent``, where a DataFrame has a column for each variable and an array or DataArray with several variables has 3 dimensions (variable by time by entity). A list, a tuple or any other container raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``exog``. It can have no variables, a DataFrame with the index of ``dependent`` and no columns or an array with 0 variables, if the model has effects. See the notes. weights : array_like, optional Weights to use in estimation. Assumes the variance of the residual is proportional to the inverse of the weight, so that the residual times the square root of the weight is homoskedastic. Weights can be given for each observation, for each time period, for each entity or for each combination of time period and entity. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. Weights with labels must use the same labels, in the same order, as dependent or, if dependent has no labels, as exog. See :ref:`panel-input-alignment`. Dependent need not be balanced when the weights are given for each time period, entity or combination: the weights of the combinations that dependent does not have are not used. A 1-d array has a value for each row of dependent, in the order of the rows, if it has as many values as dependent has rows. It has a value for each time period if it has as many values as there are time periods, and a value for each entity if it has as many as there are entities. Weights with labels (a pandas object with an index that is not the default index) are read by their labels, so that a Series indexed by the time periods has a value for each time period, and one indexed by the entities has a value for each entity. Weights without labels (an array, a list, a tuple, or a Series or a DataFrame with one column that has the default index) are read by their number of values. If dependent is not balanced and has as many rows as time periods or entities, they have a value for each row. An ``AmbiguityError`` is raised if the numbers of time periods and entities are equal and the weights have that many values, unless they have no labels and a value for each row. Any other number of values raises a ``ValueError``. entity_effects : bool, optional Flag whether to include entity (fixed) effects in the model. The default is False. time_effects : bool, optional Flag whether to include time effects in the model. The default is False. other_effects : array_like, optional Category codes to use for any effects that are not entity or time effects. Each variable is treated as an effect. An array or list with the layout of dependent (time by entity, or variable by time by entity), or a DataFrame with the time periods as its index and the entities as its columns, has a value for each time period and entity. It is placed on the rows of dependent, which need not be balanced: the values of the combinations that dependent does not have are not used (see :ref:`panel-input-alignment`). A 1-d array or list has a value for each row of dependent, in the order of the rows of dependent. An observation where any of the other effects is missing (NaN or None) is dropped, with the observations that have a missing value in dependent, exog or weights, and a ``MissingValueWarning`` is issued. singletons : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to keep singleton observations. If False, the observations that are alone in their group of an effect are dropped, repeatedly until there are none, and a ``SingletonWarning`` is issued. The weights are then scaled to have a mean of 1 in the observations that are retained. The default is True. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The weights were scaled before the singletons were dropped, so that their mean was not 1 in the retained observations and ``s2`` differed from that of the same model on data without the singletons. drop_absorbed : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to drop absorbed variables. If False, an ``AbsorbingEffectError`` is raised by ``fit`` for a model with an absorbed variable, and if True a variable is dropped with an ``AbsorbingEffectWarning``. The default is False. check_rank : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to perform a rank check on the exogenous variables to ensure that the model is identified. Skipping this check can reduce the time required to validate a model specification. Results may be numerically unstable if this check is skipped and the matrix is not full rank. The default is True. Raises ------ TypeError If `dependent` or `exog` is a container that is not supported, e.g., a list or a tuple, or if they have complex values or values that cannot be converted to float64. ValueError If `dependent`, `exog` or `weights` have different shapes or labels, if a combination of an entity and a time period appears more than once, if the weights are not strictly positive and finite or do not have a supported shape, or if `exog` does not have full column rank and `check_rank` is True. It is also raised if more than 2 effects are included, if two of the effects nest each other, if `other_effects` does not have as many entities and time periods as `dependent`, or if the model has no effects and `exog` has no columns. AmbiguityError If the numbers of time periods and entities are equal and 1-d weights have that many values, so that they could be a value for each time period or for each entity. Notes ----- Many models can be estimated. The most common included entity effects and can be described .. math:: y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta^{\prime}x_{it} + \epsilon_{it} where :math:`\alpha_i` is included if ``entity_effects=True``. Time effect are also supported, which leads to a model of the form .. math:: y_{it}= \gamma_t + \beta^{\prime}x_{it} + \epsilon_{it} where :math:`\gamma_i` is included if ``time_effects=True``. Both effects can be simultaneously used, .. math:: y_{it}=\alpha_i + \gamma_t + \beta^{\prime}x_{it} + \epsilon_{it} Additionally , arbitrary effects can be specified using categorical variables. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weights`` for each time period, each entity or each time period and entity, and ``other_effects`` for each time period and entity, can be used if ``dependent`` is not balanced. Earlier versions raised "weights must have the same number of observations as dependent" for the weights, and an error for ``other_effects``. A value for each time period and entity is placed on the rows of ``dependent`` by time period and entity. Earlier versions paired ``other_effects`` by position with the rows, which is right only if the rows are sorted by entity and then time: if they were sorted by time and then entity, an array was attached to the wrong observations without an error, and a pandas object with labels was rejected. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weights`` that are a 1-d array with a value for each row of ``dependent`` can be used if ``dependent`` is not balanced. Earlier versions raised "Weights do not have a supported shape". An array with a value for each combination of a time period and an entity is not a value for each row if ``dependent`` is not balanced. It raised an error from pandas or NumPy, e.g., "could not broadcast input array from shape (30,1) into shape (27,1)", and raises "Weights do not have a supported shape" now, which names the numbers of values that are accepted. If ``dependent`` is not balanced and has as many rows as time periods or entities, weights without labels (an array, or a Series with the default index) with that many values are a value for each row, and a Series indexed by the time periods or by the entities is a value for each time period or entity. Earlier versions raised "weights must have the same number of observations as dependent", or an ``AmbiguityError`` if the numbers of time periods and entities were equal. A DataFrame with one column and the default index is read as an array with a column is. It raised an error from pandas or NumPy if ``dependent`` was balanced, and "Weights do not have a supported shape" if it was not. A DataFrame with one column and an index that is not the default index is read as a Series with that index is, so that its labels decide. It raised "Weights do not have a supported shape". If both ``entity_effect`` and ``time_effects`` are ``False``, and no other effects are included, the model reduces to :class:`PooledOLS`. Model supports at most 2 effects. These can be entity-time, entity-other, time-other or 2 other. **Models without regressors** A model that only has effects can be estimated, .. math:: y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \epsilon_{it} where either effect can be left out. The model is created with an ``exog`` that has no columns, for example ``pd.DataFrame(index=y.index)`` or an array with 0 variables, or with a formula that has effects and no regressors, such as ``"y ~ EntityEffects"`` or ``"y ~ EntityEffects + TimeEffects"``. The formula gives the same results as ``exog`` without columns. The model has no constant, as a constant is a regressor (``"y ~ 1 + EntityEffects"`` has one). The other models, and ``PanelOLS`` without effects, raise a ``ValueError`` if ``exog`` has no columns. The results of a model without regressors are: * ``params``, ``std_errors``, ``tstats``, ``pvalues`` and ``cov`` are empty, and ``conf_int`` has no rows. The summary does not have a table of parameters, and ``wald_test`` raises a ``ValueError``. * ``estimated_effects`` are the means of the dependent variable of the entity (entity effects), of the time period (time effects), or the fitted values of the regression on the dummy variables of both effects. These are weighted means in a weighted model. There is no constant, so that the effects include the overall mean. ``fitted_values`` are 0, and ``resids`` and ``idiosyncratic`` are the dependent variable less its effects. * ``df_model`` is the number of effects, which is ``N`` for entity effects, ``T`` for time effects and ``N + T - 1`` for both, and ``df_resid`` is ``nobs`` less ``df_model``. * ``rsquared``, ``rsquared_within``, ``rsquared_between`` and ``rsquared_overall`` are 0 when they are defined, since the effects are removed from the dependent variable and there is nothing else to explain it. The squared correlations (``corr_squared_within``, ``corr_squared_between`` and ``corr_squared_overall``) are 0 as well: the fitted values of the regressors are all 0, and these measures are set to 0 if the fitted values do not vary. ``rsquared_inclusive`` is the R-squared of the effects, the share of the variation around the mean that they explain. An R-squared is not defined if the sum of squares that it divides is zero, for example ``rsquared_within`` if the dependent variable does not vary within entities. If the dependent variable is constant, there is no variation to explain and ``rsquared``, ``rsquared_within``, ``rsquared_inclusive`` and the squared correlations are NaN. * ``f_pooled`` is the test that the effects are zero. For entity effects it is the F-test of the one-way analysis of variance. ``f_statistic`` and ``f_statistic_robust``, which test the coefficients of the regressors, are ``InvalidTestStatistic`` since there are none. * ``loglik`` and ``s2`` are those of the regression on the dummy variables of the effects. ``variance_decomposition`` splits the second moment of the dependent variable, about 0 since there is no constant, into the variance of the residuals and the rest, which is attributed to the effects. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A model without regressors can be estimated. Earlier versions raised a ``ValueError`` from pandas, "No objects to concatenate", when ``exog`` had no columns or the formula had no regressors. A variable in ``exog`` is absorbed if the effects explain all of it. The algorithms that remove the effects are exact only up to rounding error, or up to a relative error of about 1e-8 if they are iterative, so a variable is treated as absorbed if less than 1e-5 of its norm is left after the effects are removed, whatever its units. It is treated in the same way if it is collinear with the variables before it once the effects are removed. An ``AbsorbingEffectError`` is raised for such a variable. If ``drop_absorbed`` is True, the variable is dropped and an ``AbsorbingEffectWarning`` is raised, and the constant is never dropped. The norm includes the mean of the variable, so a variable with a large mean and little other variation, less than 1e-5 of its norm, is also treated as absorbed. Subtract its mean to avoid this. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 An observation with a missing value in ``other_effects`` is dropped with a ``MissingValueWarning``, as it is for a missing value in ``dependent``, ``exog`` or ``weights``. Earlier versions treated a missing value as a category of its own, and ``fit`` failed after it estimated the model with the error that the observations per group cannot be computed.
