entries.name: linearmodels.SUR
entries.summary: Seemingly unrelated regression estimation (SUR/SURE).
keywords: Seemingly unrelated regression estimation (SUR/SURE). Parameters ---------- equations : dict of str to tuple or dict Dictionary-like structure containing dependent and exogenous variable values. Each key is an equations label and must be a string. Each value must be either a tuple of the form (dependent, exog, [weights]) or a dictionary with keys "dependent" and "exog" and the optional key "weights". The variables are array_like, such as lists, NumPy arrays, pandas objects and xarray DataArrays, and a ``TypeError`` that names the variable is raised for complex values or text. sigma : array_like, optional Prespecified residual covariance to use in GLS estimation, with shape (nequations, nequations). If not provided, FGLS is implemented based on an estimate of sigma. Notes ----- Estimates a set of regressions which are seemingly unrelated in the sense that separate estimation would lead to consistent parameter estimates. Each equation is of the form .. math:: y_{i,k} = x_{i,k}\beta_i + \epsilon_{i,k} where k denotes the equation and i denoted the observation index. By stacking vertically arrays of dependent and placing the exogenous variables into a block diagonal array, the entire system can be compactly expressed as .. math:: Y = X\beta + \epsilon where .. math:: Y = \left[\begin{array}{c}Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_K\end{array}\right] and .. math:: X = \left[\begin{array}{cccc} X_1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\ 0 & X_2 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & X_K \end{array}\right] The system OLS estimator is .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{OLS} = (X'X)^{-1}X'Y When certain conditions are satisfied, a GLS estimator of the form .. math:: \hat{\beta}_{GLS} = (X'\Omega^{-1}X)^{-1}X'\Omega^{-1}Y can improve accuracy of coefficient estimates where .. math:: \Omega = \Sigma \otimes I_N where :math:`\Sigma` is the covariance matrix of the residuals. SUR is a special case of 3SLS where there are no endogenous regressors and no instruments. The weights of an equation, if they are given, must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1 in the equation. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped from all of the equations. Rows are paired by position, both within an equation and across the equations. An input that carries labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates) must use the same index, in the same order, as the dependent variable of its equation, so that a value cannot be attached to the wrong observation. The dependent variables that carry labels must also use the same index in every equation. A ``ValueError`` is raised if an index differs. Either reindex the input to the index of the dependent variable, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. If none of the dependent variables carries labels, the inputs that do must use the same index as the first of them that does, in the order ``exog``, ``endog``, ``instruments`` and ``weights`` of each equation. The same rule applies to ``clusters`` passed to ``fit``. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.TradedFactorModel
entries.summary: Linear factor models estimator applicable to traded factors.
keywords: Linear factor models estimator applicable to traded factors. Parameters ---------- portfolios : array_like Test portfolio returns (nobs by nportfolio). factors : array_like Priced factor returns (nobs by nfactor). Notes ----- Implements both time-series estimators of risk premia, factor loadings and zero-alpha tests. The model estimated is .. math:: r_{it}^e = \alpha_i + f_t \beta_i + \epsilon_{it} where :math:`r_{it}^e` is the excess return on test portfolio i and :math:`f_t` are the traded factor returns. The model is directly tested using the estimated values :math:`\hat{\alpha}_i`. Risk premia, :math:`\lambda_i` are estimated using the sample averages of the factors, which must be excess returns on traded portfolios. Rows are paired by position, so that the first row of ``factors`` is the factor return in the period of the first row of ``portfolios``. If both ``portfolios`` and ``factors`` carry labels (a pandas Series or DataFrame with an index other than the default 0, 1, ..., n-1, or an xarray DataArray with coordinates), ``factors`` must use the same index, in the same order, as ``portfolios``, so that a return cannot be attached to the wrong period. A ``ValueError`` is raised if the index differs. Either reindex ``factors`` to the index of ``portfolios``, or call ``to_numpy()`` to pair its values by position. NumPy arrays and pandas objects with a default index do not carry labels and are always paired by position. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels.

entries.name: linearmodels.formula.panel_ols
entries.summary: Create a model from a formula.
keywords: Create a model from a formula. Parameters ---------- formula : str Formula to transform into model. Conforms to formulaic formula rules with two special variable names, EntityEffects and TimeEffects which can be used to specify that the model should contain an entity effect or a time effect, respectively. The formula can have effects and no regressors, for example ``"y ~ EntityEffects"``, which is a model with only entity effects that gives the same results as ``exog`` without columns. See Examples. data : PanelData or DataFrame Data structure that can be coerced into a PanelData. In most cases, this should be a multi-index DataFrame where the level 0 index contains the entities and the level 1 contains the time. A list or a tuple raises a ``TypeError`` that names ``data``. weights : array_like, optional Weights to use in estimation. Assumes the variance of the residual is proportional to the inverse of the weight, so that the residual times the square root of the weight is homoskedastic. The weights must be strictly positive and finite. They are rescaled to have a mean of 1. A NaN weight is missing, and its observation is dropped. other_effects : array_like, optional Category codes to use for any effects that are not entity or time effects. Each variable is treated as an effect. An observation where any of the other effects is missing is dropped, with a ``MissingValueWarning``. singletons : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to keep singleton observations. If False, the observations that are alone in their group of an effect are dropped, repeatedly until there are none, and a ``SingletonWarning`` is issued. The default is True. drop_absorbed : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to drop absorbed variables. If False, an ``AbsorbingEffectError`` is raised by ``fit`` for a model with an absorbed variable, and if True a variable is dropped with an ``AbsorbingEffectWarning``. The default is False. check_rank : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to perform a rank check on the exogenous variables to ensure that the model is identified. Skipping this check can reduce the time required to validate a model specification. Results may be numerically unstable if this check is skipped and the matrix is not full rank. The default is True. Returns ------- PanelOLS Model specified using the formula.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.absorbing.ClusteredCovariance
entries.summary: Covariance estimation for clustered data.
keywords: Covariance estimation for clustered data. Parameters ---------- x : ndarray Model regressors (nobs by nvar). y : ndarray Series modeled (nobs by 1). z : ndarray Instruments used for endogenous regressors (nobs by ninstr). params : ndarray Estimated model parameters (nvar by 1). clusters : array_like, optional Cluster group assignment, with shape nobs by ncluster where ncluster is 1 or 2. If not provided, every observation is its own cluster. A ``ValueError`` is raised for more columns. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to use a small-sample adjustment. The default is False. kappa : float, optional Value of kappa in the k-class estimator. The default is 1. extra_df : int, optional Degrees of freedom that the model uses in addition to the nvar columns of x, for example the absorbed effects of AbsorbingLS. The default is 0. It is only used if ``debiased`` is True, when n / (n-k) becomes n / (n-k-extra_df). Raises ------ ValueError If the number of rows of x, y and z differ, if x and params have incompatible dimensions, if clusters does not have one row for each observation or has more than 2 columns, or if ``debiased`` is True and there are no more observations than the columns of x plus ``extra_df``. Notes ----- Covariance is estimated using .. math:: n^{-1} V^{-1} \hat{S} V^{-1} where .. math:: \hat{S} & = n^{-1} (G/(G-1)) \sum_{g=1}^G \xi_{g}^\prime \xi_{g} \\ \xi_{g} & = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}_g} \hat{\epsilon}_i \hat{x}_i \\ where :math:`\hat{\gamma}=(Z'Z)^{-1}(Z'X)` and :math:`\hat{x}_i = z_i\hat{\gamma}`. :math:`\mathcal{G}_g` contains the indices of elements in cluster g. If ``debiased`` is true, then :math:`S` is scaled by g(n - 1) / ((g-1)(n-k-df)) where g is the number of groups, k is the number of columns of x and df is ``extra_df``. .. math:: V = n^{-1} X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X where :math:`X` is the matrix of variables included in the model and :math:`Z` is the matrix of instruments, including exogenous regressors.

keywords: Kernel weighted (HAC) covariance estimation. Parameters ---------- x : ndarray Model regressors (nobs by nvar). y : ndarray Series modeled (nobs by 1). z : ndarray Instruments used for endogenous regressors (nobs by ninstr). params : ndarray Estimated model parameters (nvar by 1). kernel : str, optional Kernel name. The default is "bartlett". The names are not case sensitive. Supported kernels are: * "bartlett", "newey-west" - Bartlett's kernel * "parzen", "gallant" - Parzen's kernel * "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" - Quadratic spectral kernel bandwidth : int, optional Non-negative bandwidth to use with kernel. If not provided, automatic bandwidth selection is used. It needs at least 4 observations with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel, and a ``ValueError`` is raised for fewer when the covariance is first used. See :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to use a small-sample adjustment. The default is False. kappa : float, optional Value of kappa in the k-class estimator. The default is 1. extra_df : int, optional Degrees of freedom that the model uses in addition to the nvar columns of x, for example the absorbed effects of AbsorbingLS. The default is 0. It is only used if ``debiased`` is True, when n / (n-k) becomes n / (n-k-extra_df). Raises ------ ValueError If the number of rows of x, y and z differ, if x and params have incompatible dimensions or if ``debiased`` is True and there are no more observations than the columns of x plus ``extra_df``. UnknownOptionError If ``kernel`` is not one of the supported kernels. It is both a ``KeyError`` and a ``ValueError``. See Also -------- kernel_weight_bartlett : Kernel weights from a Bartlett kernel. kernel_weight_parzen : Kernel weights from a Parzen kernel. kernel_weight_quadratic_spectral : Kernel weights from a quadratic-spectral kernel. Notes ----- Covariance is estimated using .. math:: n^{-1} V^{-1} \hat{S} V^{-1} where .. math:: \hat{S}_0 & = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{\epsilon}^2_i \hat{x}_i^{\prime} \hat{x}_{i} \\ \hat{S}_j & = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n-j} \hat{\epsilon}_i\hat{\epsilon}_{i+j} (\hat{x}_i^{\prime} \hat{x}_{i+j} + \hat{x}_{i+j}^{\prime} \hat{x}_{i}) \\ \hat{S} & = \sum_{i=0}^{bw} K(i, bw) \hat{S}_i where :math:`\hat{\gamma}=(Z'Z)^{-1}(Z'X)`, :math:`\hat{x}_i = z_i\hat{\gamma}` and :math:`K(i,bw)` is a weight that depends on the kernel. If ``debiased`` is true, then :math:`S` is scaled by n / (n-k-df), where k is the number of columns of x and df is ``extra_df``. .. math:: V = n^{-1} X'Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'X where :math:`X` is the matrix of variables included in the model and :math:`Z` is the matrix of instruments, including exogenous regressors. The automatic bandwidth is that of :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth` for the sum of the columns of :math:`\hat{\epsilon}_i \hat{x}_i`, without the column of the constant if :math:`\hat{x}` has one and other columns. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The automatic bandwidth raises a ``ValueError`` if there are fewer observations than the kernel needs, and if it is not finite. Earlier versions raised "cannot convert float infinity to integer" (an ``OverflowError``) or "cannot convert float NaN to integer" for some series, and used a bandwidth of :math:`n - 1`, or another bandwidth, for the others.

entries.summary: Kernel weights from a quadratic-spectral kernel.
keywords: Kernel weights from a quadratic-spectral kernel. Parameters ---------- bw : int or float Bandwidth of the kernel. n : int Positive number of weights to return. Returns ------- ndarray Weight array ordered by lag position (n + 1). Notes ----- Unlike the Bartlett or Parzen kernels, the QS kernel is not truncated at a specific lag, and so weights are computed for all available lags in the sample. .. math:: z_i & = 6 \pi (i / m) / 5 \\ w_0 & = 1 \\ w_i & = 3(\sin(z_i)/z_i - cos(z_i))/z_i^ 2, \, i \geq 1 where m is the bandwidth.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.cragg_donald
entries.summary: Cragg-Donald test of reduced rank for the first-stage regression.
keywords: Cragg-Donald test of reduced rank for the first-stage regression. Parameters ---------- endog : ndarray Weighted endogenous regressor array (nobs, nendog). instr : ndarray Weighted instrument array (nobs, ninstr). exog : ndarray Weighted exogenous regressor array (nobs, nexog), partialled out before testing. Include a constant column here if the model has one. Returns ------- WaldTestStatistic or InvalidTestStatistic Test statistic, distributed chi2(ninstr - nendog + 1) under the null that the first-stage coefficient matrix does not have full column rank, which is the null that the model is underidentified. An InvalidTestStatistic is returned if the statistic is not defined: when there are no endogenous regressors, fewer instruments than endogenous regressors, collinear endogenous regressors or instruments, or when the instruments predict the endogenous regressors exactly. Warnings -------- The statistic is valid only when the first-stage errors are conditionally homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated. It ignores the covariance estimator used to fit the model. If the data have heteroskedasticity, within-group dependence or serial correlation, it can reject the null of underidentification much too often. The distortion is modest with heteroskedasticity alone, but it can be very large when the instruments and the first-stage errors are both clustered or persistent. Use :func:`kleibergen_paap` with a covariance estimator that matches the dependence in the data in those cases. The null hypothesis is that the model is underidentified. Rejecting it shows that the instruments are not exactly uninformative. It does not show that they are strong. With weak instruments the asymptotic :math:`\chi^2` approximation is poor, and 2SLS can be badly biased and its tests badly sized even when the null is rejected. The p-value is asymptotic. Stock and Yogo (2005) critical values for weak instruments apply to the F form under i.i.d. errors and are not provided here. Choosing whether to use an instrumental variable estimator based on the outcome of a test like this one distorts the inference that follows. See Also -------- cragg_donald_f The F form of the statistic used with Stock-Yogo critical values. kleibergen_paap Generalization that does not require homoskedastic errors. Notes ----- Let :math:`X = Z\Pi + V`, where :math:`\Pi` is the :math:`k \times m` matrix of first-stage coefficients on the excluded instruments, after the exogenous regressors have been partialled out. The null hypothesis is :math:`\mathrm{rank}(\Pi) < m`. The statistic is the minimum eigenvalue statistic of Cragg and Donald (1993), .. math:: \mathrm{CD} = (n - k - c) \frac{r^2_{\min}}{1 - r^2_{\min}} where :math:`r_{\min}` is the smallest sample partial canonical correlation between the endogenous regressors and the excluded instruments, and :math:`c` is the number of exogenous regressors. :math:`r^2_{\min}/(1 - r^2_{\min})` is the smallest eigenvalue of :math:`(X'M_ZX)^{-1}X'P_ZX`. The statistic is asymptotically :math:`\chi^2_{k-m+1}` under the null. Anderson (1951) derived a test of the rank that is a function of the canonical correlations. The statistic is **not** the first-stage F-statistic. It equals :math:`k` times the classical F-statistic when there is a single endogenous regressor. The F form, ``CD / k``, is reported by :func:`cragg_donald_f`. **Weights.** In a weighted model, each of the arrays has to be multiplied by the square root of the observation weights, including the constant column of ``exog``. The constant is then a column of the square roots of the weights and not a column of ones, since the first-stage regressions are weighted. The sample size :math:`n` is the number of rows, and not the sum of the weights. The statistic does not change if all of the weights are multiplied by the same constant. The results of the IV models do this using weights that have been scaled to have mean 1. **Clusters.** The statistic does not use a covariance estimator, and so does not depend on clusters. It is the same for a model that is estimated with a clustered, kernel or robust covariance estimator as it is for one with an unadjusted covariance estimator. See :func:`kleibergen_paap` for a statistic that does. References ---------- Cragg, J. G., & Donald, S. G. (1993). Testing identifiability and specification in instrumental variable models. *Econometric Theory*, 9(2), 222-240. Anderson, T. W. (1951). Estimating linear restrictions on regression coefficients for multivariate normal distributions. *Annals of Mathematical Statistics*, 22(3), 327-351. Stock, J. H., & Yogo, M. (2005). Testing for weak instruments in linear IV regression. In *Identification and Inference for Econometric Models*. Cambridge University Press.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.cragg_donald_f
entries.summary: Cragg-Donald Wald F statistic.
keywords: Cragg-Donald Wald F statistic. Parameters ---------- endog : ndarray Weighted endogenous regressor array (nobs, nendog). instr : ndarray Weighted instrument array (nobs, ninstr). exog : ndarray Weighted exogenous regressor array (nobs, nexog), partialled out before testing. Include a constant column here if the model has one. Returns ------- float The Cragg-Donald statistic divided by the number of excluded instruments, or NaN if the statistic is not defined. See :func:`cragg_donald`. Warnings -------- Stock-Yogo critical values are valid only for conditionally homoskedastic, serially uncorrelated errors, and the statistic is not a test: it has no p-value. A value above a threshold does not guarantee that the instruments are strong enough for reliable inference. See the warnings in :func:`cragg_donald`. Notes ----- .. math:: F_{CD} = \frac{n - k - c}{k} \frac{r^2_{\min}}{1 - r^2_{\min}} With a single endogenous regressor this is the classical F-statistic for the joint significance of the excluded instruments in the first-stage regression. It is the statistic that Stock and Yogo (2005) tabulate critical values for. It is reported by Stata's ``ivreg2`` as the "Cragg-Donald Wald F statistic". The weights are used as in :func:`cragg_donald`. Each array, including the constant of ``exog``, is multiplied by the square root of the weights in a weighted model, and the statistic does not depend on the scale of the weights or on clusters. References ---------- Stock, J. H., & Yogo, M. (2005). Testing for weak instruments in linear IV regression. In *Identification and Inference for Econometric Models*. Cambridge University Press.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.gmm.IVGMMCovariance
entries.summary: Covariance estimation for GMM models.
keywords: Covariance estimation for GMM models. Parameters ---------- x : ndarray Model regressors (nobs by nvar). y : ndarray Series modeled (nobs by 1). z : ndarray Instruments used for endogenous regressors (nobs by ninstr). params : ndarray Estimated model parameters (nvar by 1). w : ndarray Weighting matrix used in GMM estimation (ninstr by ninstr). cov_type : str, optional Covariance estimator to use. The default is "robust". The names are not case sensitive. Supported covariance estimators are: * "unadjusted", "homoskedastic" - Assumes moment conditions are homoskedastic * "robust", "heteroskedastic" - Allows for heteroskedasticity but not autocorrelation * "kernel" - Allows for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation * "clustered" - Allows for one-way cluster dependence debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to debias the covariance estimator. The default is False. **cov_config : dict Optional keyword arguments that are specific to a particular cov_type. The keys are ``center`` (bool) for every covariance estimator, ``kernel`` (str), ``bandwidth`` (int) and ``optimal_bw`` (bool) for "kernel", and ``clusters`` (array_like) for "clustered". The names of the kernels are not case sensitive. See Notes. Raises ------ ValueError If the number of rows of x, y and z differ, or if x and params have incompatible dimensions. UnknownOptionError If ``cov_type`` is not supported. It is both a ``KeyError`` and a ``ValueError``. See Also -------- linearmodels.iv.covariance.HomoskedasticCovariance : Homoskedastic covariance. linearmodels.iv.covariance.HeteroskedasticCovariance : Heteroskedasticity robust covariance. linearmodels.iv.covariance.KernelCovariance : Kernel (HAC) covariance. linearmodels.iv.covariance.ClusteredCovariance : Clustered covariance. Notes ----- Optional keyword argument for specific covariance estimators: **kernel** * ``kernel``: Name of kernel to use. The names are not case sensitive. See :class:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.KernelCovariance` for details on available kernels * ``bandwidth``: Bandwidth to use when computing the weight. If not provided, it is selected by ``optimal_bw``. * ``optimal_bw``: Flag indicating whether to estimate the bandwidth from the data when ``bandwidth`` is not provided. If False, nobs - 2 is used. If True, the bandwidth is estimated using :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`, which needs at least 4 observations with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel, and raises a ``ValueError`` for fewer. If neither ``bandwidth`` nor ``optimal_bw`` is given, the bandwidth is estimated from the data. In 7.0 and earlier the default was ``nobs - 2``, which is not a consistent estimator of the covariance of the moment conditions. Using the default issues a ``DefaultBandwidthWarning`` (a ``UserWarning``). The previous behavior is restored by ``optimal_bw=False`` or by ``bandwidth=nobs - 2``. Passing ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw`` silences the warning, and ``optimal_bw=True`` selects the new default without it. **cluster** * ``clusters``: Array containing the cluster indices. See :class:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.ClusteredCovariance`

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix
entries.summary: Heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation robust weight estimation.
keywords: Heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation robust weight estimation. Parameters ---------- kernel : str, optional Name of kernel weighting function to use. The default is "bartlett". The names are not case sensitive. Supported kernels are: * "bartlett", "newey-west" - Bartlett's kernel * "parzen", "gallant" - Parzen's kernel * "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" - Quadratic spectral kernel bandwidth : int, optional Bandwidth to use when computing kernel weights. If not provided, the bandwidth is selected by ``optimal_bw``. center : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to center the moment conditions by subtracting the mean before computing the weight matrix. The default is False. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to use small-sample adjustments. The default is False. optimal_bw : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to estimate the bandwidth from the data when ``bandwidth`` is not provided. If False, nobs - 2 is used. If True, the bandwidth is estimated using :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`, which needs at least 4 observations with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel. The default also estimates the bandwidth, but it issues a ``DefaultBandwidthWarning`` since it changed in 7.1. See Also -------- linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_weight_bartlett : Kernel weights from a Bartlett kernel. linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_weight_parzen : Kernel weights from a Parzen kernel. linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_weight_quadratic_spectral : Kernel weights from a quadratic-spectral kernel. Notes ----- The weight matrix is .. math:: g_i & =z_i \epsilon_i \\ W & =n^{-1}(\Gamma_0+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}k(j)(\Gamma_j+\Gamma_j')) \\ \Gamma_j & =\sum_{i=j+1}^n g'_i g_{i-j} where :math:`k(j)` is the kernel weight for lag j and :math:`z_i` contains both the exogenous regressors and instruments. If neither ``bandwidth`` nor ``optimal_bw`` is given, the bandwidth is estimated from the data every time that the weight matrix is computed. In 7.0 and earlier the default was ``nobs - 2``, which is not a consistent estimator of the covariance of the moment conditions. Using the default issues a ``DefaultBandwidthWarning`` (a ``UserWarning``), once for each instance. The previous behavior is restored by ``optimal_bw=False`` or by ``bandwidth=nobs - 2``. Passing ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw`` silences the warning, and ``optimal_bw=True`` selects the new default without it. :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVGMMCUE` estimates the bandwidth once, from the residuals of the first step estimates, and uses it in every evaluation of its objective function. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weight_matrix`` raises a ``ValueError`` if the bandwidth is estimated from the data and there are fewer observations than the kernel needs (see ``optimal_bw``), or if the estimated bandwidth is not finite. Pass ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw=False`` to use the weight matrix with fewer observations. Earlier versions raised "cannot convert float infinity to integer" (an ``OverflowError``) or "cannot convert float NaN to integer" for some data when ``optimal_bw`` was True, and used a bandwidth of nobs - 1, or another bandwidth, for other data.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.gmm.kernel_optimal_bandwidth
entries.summary: Select the bandwidth of a kernel covariance estimator from the data.
keywords: Select the bandwidth of a kernel covariance estimator from the data. Parameters ---------- x : ndarray The series to use when computing the bandwidth. It has t observations, and is a 1-d array of length t or an array with t rows and 1 column. kernel : str, optional Name of the kernel to use. The default is "bartlett". The names are not case sensitive. Supported kernels are: * "bartlett", "newey-west" - Bartlett's kernel * "parzen", "gallant" - Parzen's kernel * "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" - Quadratic spectral kernel Returns ------- int Optimal bandwidth. Set to nobs - 1 if computed bandwidth is larger. Raises ------ ValueError If x has fewer observations than the kernel needs: 4 for the Bartlett kernel, 5 for the Parzen kernel and 6 for the quadratic spectral kernel. It is also raised if the bandwidth is not finite, which happens if x has values that are not finite or if the estimate of the long-run variance that the bandwidth divides by is exactly 0, as it is for a series of zeros. UnknownOptionError If kernel is not one of the supported names. It is both a ``KeyError`` and a ``ValueError``. See Also -------- kernel_weight_bartlett : Kernel weights from a Bartlett kernel. kernel_weight_parzen : Kernel weights from a Parzen kernel. kernel_weight_quadratic_spectral : Kernel weights from a quadratic-spectral kernel. Notes ----- The bandwidth is that of the nonparametric rule of Newey and West [1]_. With the autocovariances of the series :math:`x_i`, .. math:: \hat{\sigma}_j = t^{-1} \sum_{i=j+1}^{t} x_i x_{i-j}, the rule computes two weighted sums of the first :math:`n` of them, .. math:: \hat{s}_0 & = \hat{\sigma}_0 + 2 \sum_{j=1}^{n} \hat{\sigma}_j \\ \hat{s}_q & = 2 \sum_{j=1}^{n} j^q \hat{\sigma}_j and the bandwidth is the smaller of :math:`\lceil \hat{m} \rceil` and :math:`t - 1`, where .. math:: \hat{m} = c \left\{ \left(\hat{s}_q / \hat{s}_0 \right)^2 \right\}^{1 / (2q + 1)} t^{1 / (2q + 1)}. The exponent :math:`q` and the constant :math:`c` depend on the kernel. The number of lags in the pilot estimates, :math:`\hat{s}_0` and :math:`\hat{s}_q`, is :math:`n = \lceil 4 (t / 100)^a \rceil`, and the exponent :math:`a` depends on the kernel too: ===================================== = ====== ===== ============ Kernel q c a Fewest obs. ===================================== = ====== ===== ============ "bartlett", "newey-west" 1 1.1447 2/9 4 "parzen", "gallant" 2 2.6614 4/25 5 "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" 2 1.3221 2/25 6 ===================================== = ====== ===== ============ The autocovariances of a series with :math:`t` observations are defined up to lag :math:`t - 1`. If :math:`n \geq t - 1`, :math:`\hat{s}_0` is the sum of all of them, which is :math:`(\sum_i x_i)^2 / t`. It is 0, up to rounding error, for a series with a mean of 0, such as the scores of a least squares regression or the deviations of estimates from their average, so that the bandwidth divides by 0 or by rounding error. For any other series it depends on the mean alone, and not on the autocorrelation. The rule needs :math:`n < t - 1`. That is the case with at least 4 observations for the Bartlett kernel (:math:`n = 2`), 5 for the Parzen kernel (:math:`n = 3`) and 6 for the quadratic spectral kernel (:math:`n = 4`), and a ``ValueError`` is raised for fewer. Pass the bandwidth to the estimator that uses the kernel to use it with fewer observations. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A ``ValueError`` is raised if the series has fewer observations than the kernel needs, and if the bandwidth is not finite. Earlier versions raised "cannot convert float infinity to integer" (an ``OverflowError``) or "cannot convert float NaN to integer" for some series, and returned :math:`t - 1`, or another number, for the others. References ---------- .. [1] Newey, W. K. and West, K. D. (1994). Automatic lag selection in covariance matrix estimation. The Review of Economic Studies, 61(4), 631-653.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.kleibergen_paap
entries.summary: Kleibergen-Paap rk LM test of underidentification.
keywords: Kleibergen-Paap rk LM test of underidentification. Parameters ---------- endog : ndarray Weighted endogenous regressor array (nobs, nendog). instr : ndarray Weighted instrument array (nobs, ninstr). exog : ndarray Weighted exogenous regressor array (nobs, nexog), partialled out before testing. Include a constant column here if the model has one. cov_type : str, optional Covariance estimator used for the first-stage scores. The default is "robust". The names are not case sensitive. Supported covariance estimators are: * "unadjusted", "homoskedastic", "homo", "homoskedasticcovariance" - Classic homoskedastic inference * "robust", "heteroskedastic", "hccm", "heteroskedasticcovariance" - Heteroskedasticity robust inference * "kernel", "kernelcovariance" - Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation robust inference * "clustered", "one-way", "onewayclusteredcovariance" - Cluster dependent inference, which is heteroskedasticity robust cov_config : dict, optional Options for the covariance estimator. "clustered" requires ``clusters``, a 1-d array with one element for each observation. "kernel" uses ``kernel`` (default "bartlett") and ``bandwidth``. The names of the kernels are not case sensitive. If the bandwidth is not provided it is selected automatically, which needs at least 4 observations with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel. See :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`, which lists the supported kernels. Returns ------- WaldTestStatistic or InvalidTestStatistic Test statistic, distributed chi2(ninstr - nendog + 1) under the null that the first-stage coefficient matrix does not have full column rank, which is the null that the model is underidentified. An InvalidTestStatistic is returned if the statistic is not defined. See :func:`cragg_donald`. It is also returned for two-way clustering, which is not supported, for fewer than two clusters, and if the covariance of the statistic is singular. Raises ------ ValueError If ``cov_type`` is not supported, or is "clustered" and ``cov_config`` does not contain ``clusters`` or ``clusters`` does not have an element for each row of the arrays. It is also raised if ``cov_type`` is "kernel", the bandwidth is not provided and there are fewer observations than the kernel needs to select it, or the bandwidth that is selected is not finite. Warnings -------- The statistic is asymptotic. It is robust only to the extent that the chosen covariance estimator is appropriate for the data. Use "clustered" when observations are dependent within groups, and "kernel" when the data are ordered in time and the scores are autocorrelated. The data must be sorted in time order when "kernel" is used. If the dependence is not accounted for, including by "unadjusted" and "robust", the statistic can reject the null of underidentification much too often when the instruments and first-stage errors are clustered or persistent. The covariance has dimension :math:`km \times km` and is poorly estimated unless :math:`n` is large relative to :math:`km`. It is formed as a dense matrix, and so the memory that is needed grows with :math:`(km)^2`. With clustering it needs many clusters, and with few clusters the test can be very conservative. A kernel bandwidth that is too short for the dependence does not remove the over-rejection. If there are too few clusters or observations the covariance is rank deficient. A warning is issued, a generalized inverse is used and the degrees of freedom are reduced, but the result should not be relied on. The chi-square approximation is also less reliable with many instruments. The null is that the model is underidentified. Rejecting it does not show that the instruments are strong, so this is not a test for weak instruments. With weak instruments the asymptotic distribution can be a poor approximation. Choosing whether to use an instrumental variable estimator based on the outcome of a test like this one distorts the inference that follows. See Also -------- kleibergen_paap_f The F form of the statistic. cragg_donald The version that requires homoskedastic errors. Notes ----- Let :math:`\hat{\Pi}` be the :math:`k \times m` first-stage coefficient matrix after the exogenous regressors have been partialled out. The test is applied to :math:`\hat{\Theta}`, the matrix of sample partial canonical correlations between the endogenous regressors and the excluded instruments. The null is that :math:`\Theta` has rank :math:`m-1`. Let :math:`\hat{\Theta} = USV'` be a singular value decomposition, and let :math:`A_\perp` and :math:`B_\perp` contain the singular vectors of the smallest :math:`m-1` and :math:`1` singular values. The statistic is .. math:: rk = n \,\mathrm{vec}(\lambda)' \left[(B_\perp \otimes A_\perp)' \hat{V}_{\Theta} (B_\perp \otimes A_\perp)\right]^{-1} \mathrm{vec}(\lambda), \quad \lambda = A_\perp' \hat{\Theta} B_\perp where :math:`\hat{V}_\Theta` is the estimated covariance of :math:`\sqrt{n}\,\mathrm{vec}(\hat{\Theta})`. It is built from the scores :math:`x_i \otimes z_i`, where :math:`x_i` is the orthogonalized endogenous regressor and :math:`z_i` is the orthogonalized instrument, using the covariance estimator chosen by ``cov_type``. The statistic is asymptotically :math:`\chi^2_{k-m+1}` under the null. With ``cov_type`` "unadjusted" the covariance has a Kronecker structure and the statistic is Anderson's canonical correlation LM statistic, :math:`n r^2_{\min}`. No small-sample adjustment is applied to the covariance, so the ``debiased`` option of the IV models has no effect on these statistics. This is the statistic that Stata's ``ivreg2`` reports as the "Kleibergen-Paap rk LM statistic" in its underidentification test. It is computed following ``ranktest`` (Kleibergen and Schaffer). Results can differ in detail from Stata for kernel covariances since the bandwidth conventions differ: the Bartlett weight on lag :math:`j` here is :math:`1 - j/(b+1)`, so a Stata bandwidth of :math:`b+1` corresponds to a ``bandwidth`` of :math:`b`. **Weights.** In a weighted model, each of the arrays has to be multiplied by the square root of the observation weights, including the constant column of ``exog``, as for :func:`cragg_donald`. The scores are then those of the weighted first-stage regressions, and the covariance estimator is applied to them. The statistic does not change if all of the weights are multiplied by the same constant. **Clusters.** With "clustered", the scores are summed within the clusters in ``cov_config["clusters"]``. ``clusters`` has one element for each row of the arrays, in the order of the rows. It is a 1-d array, or a 2-d array with a single column. Two-way clustering is not supported. The LM statistic is a quadratic form in a covariance with :math:`k-m+1` rows, whose rank is at most the number of clusters, and so it needs at least :math:`k-m+1` clusters. The scores of the Wald F statistic of :func:`kleibergen_paap_f` sum to zero, and so it needs one more cluster. A warning is issued if there are fewer clusters. References ---------- Kleibergen, F., & Paap, R. (2006). Generalized reduced rank tests using the singular value decomposition. *Journal of Econometrics*, 133(1), 97-126. Kleibergen, F., & Schaffer, M. E. (2007). ranktest: Stata module to test the rank of a matrix using the Kleibergen-Paap rk statistic. *Statistical Software Components* S456865, Boston College.

entries.name: linearmodels.iv.kleibergen_paap_f
entries.summary: Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F statistic.
keywords: Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F statistic. Parameters ---------- endog : ndarray Weighted endogenous regressor array (nobs, nendog). instr : ndarray Weighted instrument array (nobs, ninstr). exog : ndarray Weighted exogenous regressor array (nobs, nexog), partialled out before testing. Include a constant column here if the model has one. cov_type : str, optional Covariance estimator used for the first-stage scores. The default is "robust". The names are not case sensitive. Supported covariance estimators are: * "unadjusted", "homoskedastic", "homo", "homoskedasticcovariance" - Classic homoskedastic inference * "robust", "heteroskedastic", "hccm", "heteroskedasticcovariance" - Heteroskedasticity robust inference * "kernel", "kernelcovariance" - Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation robust inference * "clustered", "one-way", "onewayclusteredcovariance" - Cluster dependent inference, which is heteroskedasticity robust cov_config : dict, optional Options for the covariance estimator. See :func:`kleibergen_paap`. Returns ------- float The rk Wald F statistic, or NaN if it is not defined. Raises ------ ValueError If ``cov_type`` is not supported, or is "clustered" and ``cov_config`` does not contain ``clusters``. It is also raised if ``cov_type`` is "kernel", the bandwidth is not provided and there are fewer observations than the kernel needs to select it, or the bandwidth that is selected is not finite. See :func:`kleibergen_paap`. Warnings -------- The statistic is a robust analogue of the Cragg-Donald F statistic, but it is **not** a test and has no p-value. Stock-Yogo critical values are derived for conditionally homoskedastic, serially uncorrelated errors and do not apply to this statistic when the errors are not i.i.d. Comparing the two is a common heuristic without a formal justification. For a single endogenous regressor, the effective F-statistic of Olea and Pflueger (2013) is a better-founded choice but is not implemented here. Even then, a large first-stage F-statistic does not ensure that confidence intervals based on 2SLS have correct coverage. The warnings in :func:`kleibergen_paap` also apply: the statistic is asymptotic, needs :math:`n` to be large relative to the number of instruments times the number of endogenous regressors, and needs many clusters if clustered. Using the statistic to decide whether to proceed with IV estimation distorts subsequent inference. Notes ----- The rk Wald statistic has the form of the statistic in :func:`kleibergen_paap`, but the scores are formed from the first-stage residuals rather than from the orthogonalized endogenous regressors. If :math:`W` is the statistic, the F statistic is .. math:: F_{rk} = \frac{W}{n} \frac{n - k - c}{k} where :math:`k` is the number of excluded instruments and :math:`c` is the number of exogenous regressors. With clustered covariance, the statistic is .. math:: F_{rk} = \frac{W}{n - 1} \frac{(n - k - c)(M - 1)}{M k} where :math:`M` is the number of clusters. With ``cov_type`` equal to "unadjusted" or "homoskedastic" the statistic is the Cragg-Donald F statistic from :func:`cragg_donald_f`. These are the definitions used by Stata's ``ivreg2`` for the "Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F statistic" (Baum, Schaffer and Stillman, 2007). The weights and clusters are used as in :func:`kleibergen_paap`. In a weighted model, each of the arrays, including the constant of ``exog``, has to be multiplied by the square root of the weights, and the statistic does not depend on their scale. The clusters have one element for each row of the arrays. If there are :math:`m` endogenous regressors, the scores of the Wald statistic sum to zero, so that at least :math:`k-m+2` clusters are needed, which is one more than for :func:`kleibergen_paap`. A warning is issued if there are fewer clusters. References ---------- Kleibergen, F., & Paap, R. (2006). Generalized reduced rank tests using the singular value decomposition. *Journal of Econometrics*, 133(1), 97-126. Olea, J. L. M., & Pflueger, C. (2013). A robust test for weak instruments. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 31(3), 358-369. Baum, C. F., Schaffer, M. E., & Stillman, S. (2007). Enhanced routines for instrumental variables/GMM estimation and testing. *Stata Journal*, 7(4), 465-506.

entries.name: linearmodels.panel.covariance.ACCovariance
entries.summary: Autocorrelation robust covariance estimation.
keywords: Autocorrelation robust covariance estimation. Parameters ---------- y : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of the dependent variable. x : ndarray (entity x time) by variables stacked array of the exogenous variables. params : ndarray Variables by 1 array of estimated model parameters. entity_ids : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of entity ids. time_ids : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of time ids. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to debias the estimator. The default is False. extra_df : int, optional Additional degrees of freedom consumed by models beyond the number of columns in x, e.g., fixed effects. Covariance estimators are always adjusted for extra_df irrespective of the setting of debiased. The default is 0. kernel : str, optional Name of the kernel. If not provided, "newey-west", which is the Bartlett kernel, is used. The names are not case sensitive. Supported kernels are: * "bartlett", "newey-west" - Bartlett's kernel * "parzen", "gallant" - Parzen's kernel * "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" - Quadratic spectral kernel bandwidth : float, optional Non-negative bandwidth to use. The Bartlett and Parzen kernels use its integer part. If not provided a rule-of-thumb value is used. It can be larger than the number of observations of an entity. Raises ------ ValueError If the model has no residual degrees of freedom: the number of observations less ``extra_df``, and less the number of regressors if ``debiased`` is True, is not positive. UnknownOptionError If ``kernel`` is not one of the supported names. It is both a ``ValueError`` and a ``KeyError``. Notes ----- Estimator is robust to autocorrelation but not cross-sectional correlation. Bandwidth is set to the common value for the Bartlett kernel if not provided, :math:`\lfloor 4 (T / 100)^{2/9} \rfloor` where :math:`T` is the number of time periods. The estimator of the covariance is .. math:: n^{-1}\hat{\Sigma}_{xx}^{-1}\hat{S}\hat{\Sigma}_{xx}^{-1} where .. math:: \hat{\Sigma}_{xx} = n^{-1}X'X and .. math:: \xi_{it} & = \epsilon_{it} x_{it} \\ \hat{S} & = (n-df)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N S_i \\ \hat{S}_i & = \sum_{j=0}^{T_i-1} K(j, bw) \hat{S}_{ij} \\ \hat{S}_{i0} & = \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} \xi'_{it} \xi_{it} \\ \hat{S}_{ij} & = \sum_{t=1}^{T_i-j} \xi'_{it} \xi_{it+j} + \xi'_{it+j} \xi_{it} where :math:`T_i` is the number of observations of entity :math:`i`, df is ``extra_df`` and n-df is replaced by n-df-k if ``debiased`` is ``True``. :math:`K(j, bw)` is the kernel weighting function, which is 1 for the lag 0. The Bartlett and Parzen kernels are 0 for the lags above ``bandwidth``. **Lags** The lag between two observations of an entity is the difference between their positions in the observations of the entity, which are in the order of time. It is not the difference between their time periods. If a period is missing between two observations of an entity, they are one lag apart. With the Bartlett kernel the covariance is that of the cluster-HAC option of statsmodels (``cov_type="hac-panel"``), which also counts positions. plm (``vcovNW``) and sandwich (``vcovPL``) pair the observations that are :math:`j` periods apart, so that their covariances are different if an entity has missing periods between its observations: in a panel where about a quarter of the periods are missing the standard errors differed by about 3%. They are the same if no entity has a gap. See :ref:`panel-ac-lags`. **Entities with few observations** An entity has the lags :math:`0,\ldots,T_i-1`, and its sum is over these lags. The weights are those of the bandwidth that was chosen, :math:`K(j, bw)`, also for an entity with fewer observations than the bandwidth. The bandwidth is not reduced to :math:`T_i-1` for such an entity, and the weights of the lags that the entity does not have are not used. This is how plm, sandwich and statsmodels compute the covariance. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The entities are not weighted by their numbers of observations: each entity contributes the sum of the products of its scores. Earlier versions divided the sum of each entity by its number of observations and averaged over the entities, which is the same for a balanced panel. For an unbalanced panel the covariance, e.g., with a bandwidth of 0, was not the heteroskedasticity robust covariance, and differed from the covariance of other packages. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 An entity with :math:`T_i` observations, where :math:`T_i \leq bw`, keeps the weights of the bandwidth. Earlier versions replaced the bandwidth of the entity by :math:`T_i-1`. This changed the Bartlett weights of the entity from :math:`1-j/(bw+1)` to :math:`1-j/T_i`, the Parzen weights in the same way, and the bandwidth of the quadratic spectral kernel. The covariance changes if any entity has fewer observations than the bandwidth, which is more likely in a panel where the entities are short or the bandwidth is large. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A ``kernel`` that is not one of the supported names raises an ``UnknownOptionError`` when the estimator is created, so that the ``fit`` method of a model raises. Earlier versions raised it when the covariance was first used, for example when ``std_errors`` of the results was read, so that ``fit`` returned results that raised when the covariance was used.

entries.name: linearmodels.panel.covariance.ClusteredCovariance
entries.summary: One-way (Rogers) or two-way clustered covariance estimation.
keywords: One-way (Rogers) or two-way clustered covariance estimation. Parameters ---------- y : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of the dependent variable. x : ndarray (entity x time) by variables stacked array of the exogenous variables. params : ndarray Variables by 1 array of estimated model parameters. entity_ids : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of entity ids. time_ids : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of time ids. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to debias the estimator. The default is False. extra_df : int, optional Additional degrees of freedom consumed by models beyond the number of columns in x, e.g., fixed effects. Covariance estimators are always adjusted for extra_df irrespective of the setting of debiased. The default is 0. clusters : array_like, optional Array of cluster group ids with nobs rows and 1 or 2 columns. If not provided, every observation is its own cluster. group_debias : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to apply small-number of groups adjustment. The default is False. Raises ------ ValueError If the model has no residual degrees of freedom: the number of observations less ``extra_df``, and less the number of regressors if ``debiased`` is True, is not positive. It is also raised if `clusters` has more than 2 columns or does not have nobs rows. Notes ----- The estimator of the covariance is .. math:: \hat{\Sigma}_{xx}^{-1}\hat{S}_{\mathcal{G}}\hat{\Sigma}_{xx}^{-1} where .. math:: \hat{\Sigma}_{xx} = X'X and :math:`\hat{S}_{\mathcal{G}}` is a one- or two-way cluster covariance of the scores. Two-way clustering is implemented by summing up the two one-way cluster covariances and then subtracting the one-way clustering covariance computed using the group formed from the intersection of the two groups. Two small sample adjustments are available. ``debiased=True`` will account for regressors in the main model. ``group_debias=True`` will provide a small sample adjustment for the number of clusters of the form .. math :: (g / (g- 1)) ((n - 1) / n) where g is the number of distinct groups and n is the number of observations.

entries.name: linearmodels.panel.covariance.DriscollKraay
entries.summary: Driscoll-Kraay heteroskedasticity-autocorrelation robust covariance estimation.
keywords: Driscoll-Kraay heteroskedasticity-autocorrelation robust covariance estimation. Parameters ---------- y : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of the dependent variable. x : ndarray (entity x time) by variables stacked array of the exogenous variables. params : ndarray Variables by 1 array of estimated model parameters. entity_ids : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of entity ids. time_ids : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of time ids. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to debias the estimator. The default is False. extra_df : int, optional Additional degrees of freedom consumed by models beyond the number of columns in x, e.g., fixed effects. Covariance estimators are always adjusted for extra_df irrespective of the setting of debiased. The default is 0. kernel : str, optional Name of the kernel. If not provided, "newey-west", which is the Bartlett kernel, is used. The names are not case sensitive. Supported kernels are: * "bartlett", "newey-west" - Bartlett's kernel * "parzen", "gallant" - Parzen's kernel * "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" - Quadratic spectral kernel bandwidth : float, optional Non-negative bandwidth to use. It must be below the number of time periods. The Bartlett and Parzen kernels use its integer part. If not provided a rule-of-thumb value is used. Raises ------ ValueError If the bandwidth, or the default bandwidth if none is given, is not below the number of time periods. It is also raised if the model has no residual degrees of freedom: the number of observations less ``extra_df``, and less the number of regressors if ``debiased`` is True, is not positive. UnknownOptionError If ``kernel`` is not one of the supported names. It is both a ``ValueError`` and a ``KeyError``. Notes ----- Bandwidth is set to the common value for the Bartlett kernel if not provided, :math:`\lfloor 4 (T / 100)^{2/9} \rfloor` where :math:`T` is the number of time periods. The estimator of the covariance is .. math:: n^{-1}\hat{\Sigma}_{xx}^{-1}\hat{S}\hat{\Sigma}_{xx}^{-1} where .. math:: \hat{\Sigma}_{xx} = n^{-1}X'X and .. math:: \xi_t & = \sum_{i=1}^{n_t} \epsilon_i x_{i} \\ \hat{S}_0 & = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \xi'_t \xi_t \\ \hat{S}_j & = \sum_{i=1}^{t-j} \xi'_t \xi_{t+j} + \xi'_{t+j} \xi_t \\ \hat{S} & = (n-df)^{-1} \sum_{j=0}^{bw} K(j, bw) \hat{S}_j where df is ``extra_df`` and n-df is replaced by n-df-k if ``debiased`` is ``True``. :math:`K(i, bw)` is the kernel weighting function. The sums :math:`\xi_t` of the scores of the :math:`T` time periods have autocovariances up to lag :math:`T-1`, so the bandwidth must be below :math:`T`. The bandwidth is checked when the estimator is created, so that the ``fit`` method of a model raises the error. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A bandwidth that is not below the number of time periods raises a ``ValueError``. Earlier versions raised "Length of w is larger than the number of elements in z" with the Bartlett and Parzen kernels, when the covariance was first used. The quadratic spectral kernel, which has no truncation, returned a covariance without an error. With a large bandwidth the weights of all of the lags are close to one, and the sum of the scores over all of the periods is zero in a regression, so that the covariance was close to zero. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A ``kernel`` that is not one of the supported names raises an ``UnknownOptionError`` when the estimator is created, so that the ``fit`` method of a model raises. Earlier versions raised it when the covariance was first used, for example when ``std_errors`` of the results was read, so that ``fit`` returned results that raised when the covariance was used.

entries.name: linearmodels.panel.covariance.FamaMacBethCovariance
entries.summary: HAC estimator for Fama-MacBeth estimator.
keywords: HAC estimator for Fama-MacBeth estimator. Parameters ---------- y : ndarray (entity x time) by 1 stacked array of the dependent variable. x : ndarray (entity x time) by variables stacked array of the exogenous variables. params : ndarray (variables by 1) array of estimated model parameters. all_params : DataFrame (nobs by variables) array of all estimated model parameters. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to debias the estimator. The default is False. bandwidth : float, optional Non-negative bandwidth to use. It must be below T, the number of time periods that are used. The Bartlett and Parzen kernels use its integer part. Set to 0 to disable autocorrelation robustness. If not provided, it is computed from the T estimates and is at most T - 1. The computation needs at least 4 time periods with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel. See :func:`~linearmodels.iv.covariance.kernel_optimal_bandwidth`. kernel : str, optional Name of the kernel. If not provided, "newey-west", which is the Bartlett kernel, is used. The names are not case sensitive. Supported kernels are: * "bartlett", "newey-west" - Bartlett's kernel * "parzen", "gallant" - Parzen's kernel * "qs", "quadratic-spectral", "andrews" - Quadratic spectral kernel Raises ------ ValueError If the bandwidth is not below the number of time periods that are used. It is also raised if the bandwidth is not provided and there are fewer time periods than the kernel needs to compute it, or if the bandwidth that is computed is not finite. UnknownOptionError If ``kernel`` is not one of the supported names, whether or not the covariance is a kernel covariance. It is both a ``ValueError`` and a ``KeyError``. Notes ----- Covariance is a Kernel covariance of all estimated parameters. The :math:`T` cross-sectional estimates, one for each time period that is used, have autocovariances up to lag :math:`T-1`, so the bandwidth must be below :math:`T`. The bandwidth is checked, or computed if it is not provided, when the estimator is created, so that the ``fit`` method of the model raises the error. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A bandwidth that is not below the number of time periods raises a ``ValueError``. Earlier versions raised "Length of w is larger than the number of elements in z" with the Bartlett and Parzen kernels, when the covariance was first used. The quadratic spectral kernel, which has no truncation, returned a covariance without an error. With a large bandwidth the weights of all of the lags are close to one, and the deviations of the estimates from their average sum to zero, so that the covariance was close to zero. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 The bandwidth that is computed from the estimates needs at least 4 time periods with the Bartlett kernel, 5 with the Parzen kernel and 6 with the quadratic spectral kernel, and a ``ValueError`` is raised for fewer, when the estimator is created. The deviations of the estimates from their average sum to zero. With fewer periods the rule divides by the sum of all of their autocovariances, which is zero, so that earlier versions raised "cannot convert float infinity to integer" (an ``OverflowError``) or "cannot convert float NaN to integer" when the covariance was first used, or used a bandwidth of :math:`T-1` because of the rounding error of the sum. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 A ``kernel`` that is not one of the supported names raises an ``UnknownOptionError`` when the estimator is created, so that the ``fit`` method of the model raises, also if the bandwidth is given. Earlier versions raised it when the covariance was first used, for example when ``std_errors`` of the results was read, so that ``fit`` returned results that raised when the covariance was used.

entries.name: linearmodels.panel.data.PanelData
entries.summary: Abstraction to handle alternative formats for panel data.
keywords: Abstraction to handle alternative formats for panel data. Parameters ---------- x : DataFrame, Series, ndarray, DataArray or PanelData Input data. A list or a tuple raises a ``TypeError``, since the layout of the data would not be known. A ``TypeError`` is also raised if the data are complex or cannot be converted to float64. var_name : str, optional Variable name to use when naming variables in NumPy arrays or xarray DataArrays. The default is ``"x"``. convert_dummies : bool, optional Flag indicating whether pandas categoricals or string input data should be converted to dummy variables. The default is True. drop_first : bool, optional Flag indicating to drop first dummy category when converting. The default is True. copy : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to copy the input. Only has an effect when x is a DataFrame with a MultiIndex. The default is True. Raises ------ TypeError If the input type is not supported, or if it is complex or cannot be converted to float64. ValueError If the input has the wrong number of dimensions or a MultiIndex DataFrame does not have 2 levels, if the time labels are neither numbers nor dates, or if a combination of an entity and a time period appears more than once. Notes ----- Data can be either 2- or 3-dimensional. The three key dimensions are * nvar - number of variables * nobs - number of time periods * nentity - number of entities All 3-d inputs should be in the form (nvar, nobs, nentity). With one exception, 2-d inputs are treated as (nobs, nentity) so that the input can be treated as-if being (1, nobs, nentity). If the 2-d input is a pandas DataFrame with a 2-level MultiIndex then the input is treated differently. Index level 0 is assumed to be entity. Index level 1 is time. The columns are the variables. MultiIndex Series are also accepted and treated as single column MultiIndex DataFrames. The data can have no variables, a DataFrame with a MultiIndex and no columns or an array with 0 variables. It is the ``exog`` of a :class:`~linearmodels.panel.model.PanelOLS` model that only has effects. The means, counts and demeaned data have no variables either. Missing values (NaN) in the entity or time index are not supported. The methods that group by the index raise a ValueError if the level that they use has a missing label. The time labels must be numbers or dates. A pandas ``PeriodIndex`` is accepted: it is converted with ``to_timestamp()``, so that the time labels are the timestamps at the start of the periods, and the data are the same as those of a panel that is indexed by timestamps. Each combination of an entity and a time period can appear only once, since an observation is identified by them. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 Duplicated (entity, time) rows raise a ``ValueError``. Earlier versions accepted them, except for the first difference estimator, which raised an error from pandas, and the other estimators treated them as separate observations. A ``PeriodIndex`` of time labels is accepted. Earlier versions raised a ``ValueError`` that the time labels must be numeric or date-like.

Parameters ---------- cats : DataFrame or array_like Array containing the category codes of pandas categoricals with shape (nobs, ncats). A DataFrame must only contain categoricals. An array is converted with ``np.asarray`` and must have 2 dimensions. output_format : {"csc", "csr", "coo"}, optional Format of the sparse output. The default is "csc". The formats are: * "csc" - sparse array in compressed column form (csc_array) * "csr" - sparse array in compressed row form (csr_array) * "coo" - sparse array in coordinate form (coo_array) drop : {"first", "last"}, optional Exclude either the first or last category. This only applies when cats contains more than one column, unless `drop_all` is True. The default is "first". drop_all : bool, optional Flag indicating whether all sets of dummies should exclude one category. The default is False. precondition : bool, optional Flag indicating whether the columns of the dummy matrix should be preconditioned to have unit 2-norm. The default is True. Returns ------- dummies : csc_array or csr_array or coo_array Sparse array, with the format set by `output_format`, of size nobs by ndummies containing the dummy variable values. cond : ndarray Conditioning number of each column. Raises ------ TypeError If cats is a DataFrame with a column that is not categorical. ValueError If cats is an array that does not have 2 dimensions, or if `output_format` is not one of the supported formats.

It is always retained, and the other columns are compared with it first. x_orig : ndarray, optional Regressors before the effects were absorbed, with the same shape as x. entries.name: linearmodels.shared.alignment.check_alignment
entries.summary: Reject labelled inputs whose row index is not the expected index.
keywords: Reject labelled inputs whose row index is not the expected index. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions are the same labels. See ``same_labels``. Parameters ---------- expected : Index or None Labels of the rows of the reference, usually dependent. If None, the reference does not carry labels, and the first input that carries labels is the reference instead. inputs : dict of str to object or iterable of tuple of (str, object) The inputs to check, keyed by the name to use in the message, or pairs of the name and the input, in the order of the arguments. Inputs that are None or do not carry labels are not checked. reference : str, optional Description of the input that sets the labels. The default is "dependent". Raises ------ ValueError If the labels of an input differ from the expected labels. See Also -------- row_labels : Row labels of an input, if it carries labels. reference_labels : The labels that the inputs have to use.

keywords: Reject labelled inputs whose row index is not the index of the reference. Estimation pairs rows by position. An input with the same values in a different order would attach those values to the wrong observation. Inputs with a different number of rows are not checked here since these are reported using a length-specific error message. A default index has no labels and is paired by position. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, so that the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels. See ``same_labels``. Parameters ---------- name : str Description of the input, which is used in the message. labels : Index Labels of the rows of the input. expected : Index Labels of the rows of the reference. reference : str, optional Description of the input that sets the labels. The default is "dependent". Raises ------ ValueError If the labels differ from the expected labels.

Parameters ---------- value : object The input to check. columns : bool, optional Whether the columns of a DataFrame also carry labels, so that a DataFrame with a default index and non-default columns is labelled. entries.summary: The labels that the inputs have to use, and the input that they belong to.
keywords: The labels that the inputs have to use, and the input that they belong to. The dependent variable sets the labels if it carries labels. If it does not, the first of the inputs that carries labels sets them, so that two inputs that carry labels cannot be attached to the wrong observations either. Parameters ---------- expected : Index or None Labels of the rows of the dependent variable. None if the dependent variable does not carry labels. inputs : dict of str to object or iterable of tuple of (str, object) The inputs in order, keyed by the name to use in the message. Inputs that are None or do not carry labels are not considered. The same name can be used more than once if the inputs are given as pairs. reference : str, optional Description of the dependent variable. The default is "dependent". entries.name: linearmodels.shared.alignment.same_labels
entries.summary: Whether two sets of labels are the same, where dates are compared by value.
keywords: Whether two sets of labels are the same, where dates are compared by value. The labels are the same if they have the same values in the same order. Dates and time deltas are compared by value, and so the same dates at different resolutions, e.g., ``datetime64[us]`` and ``datetime64[ns]``, are the same labels. ``Index.equals`` treats them in this way in pandas 3, but not in pandas 2. Parameters ---------- labels : Index The labels to check. expected : Index The expected labels. Returns ------- bool True if labels has the same values in the same order as expected. Notes ----- Dates and time deltas are compared at the finer of their resolutions. A value that cannot be represented at that resolution, e.g., a date in the year 3000 in nanoseconds, cannot be in the index that has the finer resolution, and so the labels are different. The levels of a ``MultiIndex`` are compared in the same way. Everything else is compared as by ``Index.equals``, so that dates in different time zones, and dates with and without a time zone, are different labels as they are in pandas 3.

entries.name: linearmodels.shared.exceptions.DefaultBandwidthWarning
entries.summary: Warning that a kernel estimator uses the bandwidth that it selects by default.
keywords: Warning that a kernel estimator uses the bandwidth that it selects by default. This warning will be removed in linearmodels 8.0, when the estimated bandwidth has been the default for a release. Notes ----- The default bandwidth of the kernel estimators of the covariance of the moment conditions used by :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVGMM`, :class:`~linearmodels.iv.model.IVGMMCUE` and :class:`~linearmodels.system.model.IVSystemGMM` changed in linearmodels 7.1. When neither ``bandwidth`` nor ``optimal_bw`` is given, the bandwidth is now estimated from the data. Earlier versions used ``nobs - 2``, which is not a consistent estimator of the covariance. The estimates, standard errors and J statistic can differ from those of earlier versions. The warning is a ``UserWarning``, so it is shown by default. It is issued once by each call to ``fit`` that uses the new default for the weight matrix (``weight_type="kernel"``) or, in ``IVGMM`` and ``IVGMMCUE``, for the parameter covariance (``cov_type="kernel"``), and once by a :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix`, :class:`~linearmodels.system.gmm.KernelWeightMatrix` or :class:`~linearmodels.iv.gmm.IVGMMCovariance` that is used directly. ``IVSystemGMM`` estimated the bandwidth of its kernel covariance from the data before, and so only its weight matrix uses a new default. Pass ``optimal_bw=False`` or ``bandwidth=nobs - 2`` to restore the previous bandwidth. Passing ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw`` silences the warning, and ``optimal_bw=True`` keeps the new default.

entries.name: linearmodels.shared.hypotheses.NormalTestStatistic
entries.summary: Test statistic holder for tests with an asymptotic standard normal law.
keywords: Test statistic holder for tests with an asymptotic standard normal law. Parameters ---------- stat : float The test statistic. null : str A statement of the test's null hypothesis. name : str, optional Name of test. two_sided : bool, optional Flag indicating whether p-values and critical values are computed using a two-sided test. The default is True. Notes ----- A two-sided test rejects the null if the absolute value of the statistic :math:`s` is large. The p-value is :math:`2\Pr(Z > |s|)`, where :math:`Z` has a standard normal distribution, and the critical values for tests of size 10%, 5% and 1% are the 0.95, 0.975 and 0.995 quantiles of the standard normal. A one-sided test rejects the null if the statistic is large. The p-value is :math:`\Pr(Z > s)`, which is close to 1 if the statistic is large and negative, and the critical values are the 0.9, 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles.

entries.name: linearmodels.shared.hypotheses.quadratic_form_test
entries.summary: Test linear equality constraints using a Wald test.
keywords: Test linear equality constraints using a Wald test. Parameters ---------- params : array_like Parameter estimates with p elements. It must be a Series, indexed by the names of the parameters, if ``formula`` is used. cov : array_like Covariance of the parameter estimates, with shape (p, p). restriction : array_like, optional Array with q rows and p columns containing linear weights to apply to parameters when forming the restrictions. It is not possible to use both ``restriction`` and ``formula``. value : array_like, optional Array with q elements containing the restricted values. The default is zeros. formula : str, list of str or dict of str to float, optional Linear constraints in the formulaic syntax. The names in the constraints are the entries of the index of ``params``. It is one of: * A single comma-separated string such as "x1=0, x2+x3=1" * A list of strings where each element is a single constraint such as ["x1=0", "x2+x3=1"] * A single string without commas to test simple constraints such as "x1=x2=x3=0" * A dictionary where each key is a parameter restriction and the corresponding value is the restriction value, e.g., {"x1": 0, "x2+x3": 1}. Returns ------- WaldTestStatistic Test statistic for the null that the restrictions are valid. It has a chi-squared distribution with q degrees of freedom. Raises ------ ValueError If both ``restriction`` and ``formula`` are provided, or if a string constraint does not contain an equal sign. TypeError If ``formula`` is used and ``params`` is not a Series, or if the value of a constraint cannot be converted to a float. Notes ----- The null hypothesis is :math:`H_0:C\theta=v`, where the matrix C is ``restriction`` and v is ``value``. The statistic is :math:`(C\hat\theta-v)'(C\hat\Sigma C')^{-1}(C\hat\theta-v)`, where :math:`\hat\Sigma` is ``cov``.

keywords: Check whether the columns of an array contain a constant or span one. Parameters ---------- x : array_like Array to be checked for a constant, with shape (nobs, nvar). x_rank : int, optional Not used. The rank of x is found when the constant is searched for, and a value that is not the rank would change the answer. It is accepted so that existing calls continue to work. Returns ------- const : bool Flag indicating whether x contains a constant or has column span with a constant. loc : int Column location of the constant, which is -1 if there is no constant. If the constant is not a column, the location is that of the column that varies the least relative to its size. Notes ----- A constant is explicit if a column has the same value in every row. Its location is that of the first column of ones, and if there is none, that of the first other column with a single value. Otherwise, x has an implicit constant if the column of ones is in the column space of x, for example, if the columns include the dummy variables for every category of a variable. The test is exact for any rank of x. The columns are scaled to have a largest absolute value of 1, which does not change the column space, and the column of ones is regressed on them using a least squares solver based on the singular value decomposition, which ignores the directions that the columns do not span. The column of ones is in the column space if the norm of the residual, relative to the norm of the column of ones, is no larger than the square root of the machine precision, about 1.5e-8. This ratio is the sine of the angle between the column of ones and the column space. It is 0 if the column of ones is in the column space and is of the order of 1 for most data. The rounding error in the ratio is about the machine precision times the condition number of the scaled columns, so that the tolerance allows condition numbers up to about 1e8. A column that differs from a constant by less than the tolerance, relative to its size, is read as a constant. If the rank of x is the number of rows, its columns span every column, and so also the column of ones. This is not read as a constant.

entries.name: linearmodels.shared.rsquared.total_ss_is_zero
entries.summary: Check if a total sum of squares is zero, up to rounding error.
keywords: Check if a total sum of squares is zero, up to rounding error. Parameters ---------- total_ss : float The total sum of squares, which is centered if the model has a constant. y_ss : float The sum of squares of the dependent variable, with the weights of the model and without removing a mean or the effects. It sets the size of the rounding error in ``total_ss``. For a total sum of squares that is not centered it is the total sum of squares. nobs : int The number of observations that ``total_ss`` adds. Returns ------- bool True if ``total_ss`` is no larger than ``(max(nobs, 100) * eps) ** 2 * y_ss``, where ``eps`` is the machine precision. Notes ----- A dependent variable that does not vary has a total sum of squares of 0, or a positive number that is only rounding error, e.g., the mean of a variable that is always 0.1 is not exactly 0.1. The sum of n numbers is off by at most about ``n * eps`` times the sum of their absolute values, however it is computed. The mean of n copies of c can then differ from c by ``n * eps * |c|``, so that every deviation from the mean has that size, and the sum of their squares is ``(n * eps) ** 2 * y_ss``, since ``y_ss`` is ``n * c ** 2``. A total sum of squares that is no larger is rounding error. Effects, quasi-differences and weights have the same bound. The rounding error that was observed in the models was smaller, at most 0.007 ``n * eps`` for a variable that is constant, with 2 million observations in a model with effects, which sum the data one after the other, and a few ``eps`` with fewer than 1,000 observations or when the sums are computed in pairs. At least 100 is used for ``n`` since the error does not become smaller than that of a few additions. A variable that varies in the data has a total sum of squares that is larger than the limit unless its standard deviation is smaller than ``n * eps`` times its root mean square, which is 2.2e-10 with a million observations, and which cannot be told from rounding error in the sum.

A NaN is a missing value, which is ignored in the mean and remains a NaN. Returns ------- ndarray The weights divided by their mean, with the shape of weights. Notes ----- The weights are divided by the largest weight, and then by the mean of the result. The mean of the weights can overflow, e.g., the sum of 10 weights of 1e308 is infinite, so that dividing by it gives weights of 0, but the mean of weights that are at most 1 cannot. The result is finite for any finite weights: it is at most the number of weights. A weight that is smaller than the largest weight by a factor of more than about 1e323 is 0 after the division by the largest weight. entries.summary: Clustered covariance estimation for system regression.
keywords: Clustered covariance estimation for system regression. Parameters ---------- x : list of ndarray Regressors of each equation, with shape (nobs, k_i) for equation i. eps : ndarray Model residuals, with shape (nobs, neq). sigma : ndarray Covariance of the residuals of the equations that is used to weight the equations if ``gls`` is True, with shape (neq, neq). full_sigma : ndarray Covariance of the residuals of the equations at the final estimates, with shape (neq, neq). It differs from ``sigma`` if the weights are not the covariance of the final residuals, e.g., if the model was given ``sigma`` or did not iterate. It is used to estimate the covariance of the scores if ``gls`` is True. gls : bool, optional Flag indicating to compute the GLS covariance estimator. If False, assume OLS was used. The default is False. debiased : bool, optional Flag indicating to apply a small sample adjustment. The default is False. constraints : LinearConstraint, optional Constraints used in estimation. The default is no constraints. clusters : array_like, optional Array of cluster ids. It must be integer valued, and have shape (nobs,) or (nobs, ncluster) where ncluster is 1 or 2. The default is no clusters, which gives the heteroskedasticity robust covariance. group_debias : bool, optional Flag indicating whether to debias by the number of groups. The default is False. See Also -------- linearmodels.shared.covariance.cov_cluster Core cluster covariance estimator. linearmodels.shared.covariance.group_debias_coefficient Scale that debiases a covariance by the number of groups. Notes ----- If GLS is used, the covariance is estimated by .. math:: (X'\Omega^{-1}X)^{-1}\tilde{S}_{\mathcal{G}}(X'\Omega^{-1}X)^{-1} where X is a block diagonal matrix of exogenous variables and where :math:`\tilde{S}_{\mathcal{G}}` is a clustered estimator of the model scores based on the model residuals and the weighted X matrix :math:`\Omega^{-1/2}X`. When GLS is not used, the covariance is estimated by .. math:: (X'X)^{-1}\hat{S}_{\mathcal{G}}(X'X)^{-1} where :math:`\hat{S}` is a clustered estimator of the covariance of the model scores.

Notes ----- The weight matrix estimator is .. math:: W & = \hat{\Gamma}_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} w_i (\hat{\Gamma}_i+\hat{\Gamma}_i^\prime) \\ \hat{\Gamma}_j & = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-j} g'_ig_{i+j} \\ g_i & = (z_{1i}\epsilon_{1i},z_{2i}\epsilon_{2i},\ldots,z_{ki}\epsilon_{ki}) where :math:`g_i` is the vector of scores across all equations for observation i and :math:`w_j` are the kernel weights which depend on the selected kernel and bandwidth. :math:`z_{ji}` is the vector of instruments for equation j and :math:`\epsilon_{ji}` is the error for equation j for observation i. This form allows for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation between the moment conditions. If neither ``bandwidth`` nor ``optimal_bw`` is given, the bandwidth is estimated from the data every time that the weight matrix is computed. In 7.0 and earlier the default was ``nobs - 2``, which is not a consistent estimator of the covariance of the moment conditions. Using the default issues a ``DefaultBandwidthWarning`` (a ``UserWarning``), once for each instance. The previous behavior is restored by ``optimal_bw=False`` or by ``bandwidth=nobs - 2``. Passing ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw`` silences the warning, and ``optimal_bw=True`` selects the new default without it. .. versionchanged:: 7.1 ``weight_matrix`` raises a ``ValueError`` if the bandwidth is estimated from the data and there are fewer observations than the kernel needs (see ``optimal_bw``), or if the estimated bandwidth is not finite. Pass ``bandwidth`` or ``optimal_bw=False`` to use the weight matrix with fewer observations. Earlier versions raised "cannot convert float infinity to integer" (an ``OverflowError``) or "cannot convert float NaN to integer" for some data when ``optimal_bw`` was True, and used a bandwidth of nobs - 1, or another bandwidth, for other data.
